Kotlin Multiplatform documentation has moved to kotlinlang.org. Now you can switch between Kotlin and KMP docs in one place. We've also refreshed the table of contents for the language guide and introduced new navigation.

Other notable changes since the last Kotlin release:

KMP overview – explore the Kotlin Multiplatform ecosystem on a single page.

Kotlin Multiplatform quickstart – learn how to set up an environment with the KMP IDE plugin.

What's new in Compose Multiplatform 1.9.3 – learn about the highlights from the latest release.

Get started with Kotlin/JS – create a web application for the browser using Kotlin/JavaScript.

Classes – learn the basics and best practices of using classes in Kotlin.

Extensions – learn how you can extend classes and interfaces in Kotlin.

Coroutines basics – explore key coroutine concepts and learn how to create your first coroutines.

Cancellation and timeouts – learn how coroutine cancellation works and how to make coroutines respond to cancellation.

Kotlin/Native libraries – see how to produce klib library artifacts.

Kotlin Notebook overview – create interactive notebook documents with the Kotlin Notebook plugin.

Add Kotlin to a Java project – configure a Java project to use both Kotlin and Java.

Test Java code with Kotlin – test a mixed Java-Kotlin project with JUnit.

New case studies page – discover how different companies apply Kotlin.

Language

After the Kotlin 2.0.0 release with the K2 compiler, the JetBrains team is focusing on improving the language with new features. In this release, we are excited to announce several new language design improvements.

These features are available in preview, and we encourage you to try them and share your feedback:

Guard conditions in when with a subject

Non-local break and continue

Multi-dollar interpolation: improved handling of $ in string literals

All the features have IDE support in the latest 2024.3 version of IntelliJ IDEA with K2 mode enabled.

Learn more in the IntelliJ IDEA 2024.3 blog post .

See the full list of Kotlin language design features and proposals .

This release also brings the following language updates:

Support for requiring opt-in to extend APIs

Improved overload resolution for functions with generic types

Improved exhaustiveness checks for when expressions with sealed classes

candidates.text:
Breaking changes and deprecations

This section highlights important breaking changes and deprecations. For a complete overview, see our Compatibility guide .

Starting with Kotlin 2.3.0, the compiler no longer supports -language-version=1.8 . There's also no support for -language-version=1.9 on non-JVM platforms.

Language feature sets older than 2.0 (excluding 1.9 for the JVM platform) aren't supported, but the language itself remains fully backward-compatible with Kotlin 1.0.

If you use both the kotlin-dsl and the kotlin("jvm") plugin in your Gradle project, you may see a Gradle warning about an unsupported Kotlin plugin version. See our compatibility guide for guidance on migration steps.

In Kotlin Multiplatform, support for the Android target is now available through Google's com.android.kotlin.multiplatform.library plugin . Migrate your projects with Android targets to the new plugin and rename your androidTarget blocks to android .

If you continue using the Kotlin Multiplatform Gradle plugin for Android targets with Android Gradle plugin (AGP) 9.0.0 or later, you see a configuration error when using the androidTarget block, along with diagnostic messages that provide guidance on how to migrate. You can avoid this error by using AGP 8.x and updating to Kotlin 2.3.10, or by migrating to Google's plugin for Android targets .

AGP 9.0.0 includes built-in support for Kotlin . Starting with Kotlin 2.3.0, you see a configuration error if you use this version of AGP with the kotlin-android plugin , because the plugin is no longer necessary. New diagnostic messages are available to help you migrate. If you use older AGP versions, you see a deprecation warning.

To align Kotlin Multiplatform with upcoming changes in Gradle, we are phasing out the withJava() function. Java source sets are now created by default . If you use the Java test fixtures Gradle plugin, upgrade directly to Kotlin 2.1.21 to avoid compatibility issues.

The JetBrains team is proceeding with the deprecation of the kotlin-android-extensions plugin. If you try to use it in your project, you'll now get a configuration error, and no plugin code will be executed.

The legacy kotlin.incremental.classpath.snapshot.enabled property has been removed from the Kotlin Gradle plugin. The property used to provide an opportunity to fall back to a built-in ABI snapshot on the JVM. The plugin now uses other methods to detect and avoid unnecessary recompilations, making the property obsolete.

This section highlights important breaking changes and deprecations. For more information about deprecations in Kotlin 2.3.0 and 2.3.20, see the Compatibility guide .

In Kotlin 2.3.20, Kotlin/Wasm performs module initialization as part of the Wasm module's instantiation, instead of relying on external JavaScript to call an _initialize() function afterward. This change makes Kotlin/Wasm more independent and prepares it for the ES module integration proposal .

If you use the @EagerInitialization annotation, related code may fail if it runs before module initialization completes. We recommend avoiding using the @EagerInitialization annotation unless you truly need it.

Changes to context-sensitive resolution

Context-sensitive resolution is still Experimental , but we are continually improving the feature based on user feedback:

The sealed and enclosing supertypes of the current type are now considered part of the contextual scope of the search. No other supertype scopes are considered. See the KT-77823 YouTrack issue for motivation and examples.

When type operators and equalities are involved, the compiler now reports a warning if using context-sensitive resolution makes the resolution ambiguous. This can happen, for example, when a clashing declaration of a class is imported. See the KT-77821 YouTrack issue for motivation and examples.

candidates.text:
Documentation updates

Kotlin Multiplatform documentation has moved to kotlinlang.org. Now you can switch between Kotlin and KMP docs in one place. We've also refreshed the table of contents for the language guide and introduced new navigation.

Other notable changes since the last Kotlin release:

KMP overview – explore the Kotlin Multiplatform ecosystem on a single page.

Kotlin Multiplatform quickstart – learn how to set up an environment with the KMP IDE plugin.

What's new in Compose Multiplatform 1.9.3 – learn about the highlights from the latest release.

Get started with Kotlin/JS – create a web application for the browser using Kotlin/JavaScript.

Classes – learn the basics and best practices of using classes in Kotlin.

Extensions – learn how you can extend classes and interfaces in Kotlin.

Coroutines basics – explore key coroutine concepts and learn how to create your first coroutines.

Cancellation and timeouts – learn how coroutine cancellation works and how to make coroutines respond to cancellation.

Kotlin/Native libraries – see how to produce klib library artifacts.

Kotlin Notebook overview – create interactive notebook documents with the Kotlin Notebook plugin.

Add Kotlin to a Java project – configure a Java project to use both Kotlin and Java.

Test Java code with Kotlin – test a mixed Java-Kotlin project with JUnit.

New case studies page – discover how different companies apply Kotlin.

candidates.text:
Prohibit delegating a Kotlin interface to a Java class when the generic signatures don't match

Issue : KTLC-267

Component : Core language

Incompatible change type : source

Short summary : Kotlin 2.3.0 forbids delegation to a Java class that implements a generic interface method with a non-generic override. Previously, allowing this behavior led to type mismatches and ClassCastException reported at runtime. This change shifts the error from runtime to compile time.

Deprecation cycle :

2.1.20: report a warning

2.3.0: raise the warning to an error

candidates.text:
How to enable

To use named-based destructuring in your project, add the compiler option to your build configuration file:

kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.add("-Xname-based-destructuring=only-syntax")
    }
}

<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.jetbrains.kotlin</groupId>
            <artifactId>kotlin-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            <configuration>
                <args>
                    <arg>-Xname-based-destructuring=only-syntax</arg>
                </args>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

Opting in to name-based destructuring also introduces a new syntax for position-based destructuring using square brackets:

// Uses explicit position-based destructuring
val [username, email] = user

We plan to gradually move toward destructuring declarations using name-based matching by default, while preserving position-based destructuring with the new square bracket syntax.

candidates.text:
ArrayDeque

ArrayDeque<T> is an implementation of a double-ended queue, which allows you to add or remove elements both at the beginning or end of the queue. As such, ArrayDeque also fills the role of both a Stack and Queue data structure in Kotlin. Behind the scenes, ArrayDeque is realized using a resizable array that automatically adjusts in size when required:

fun main() {
    val deque = ArrayDeque(listOf(1, 2, 3))

    deque.addFirst(0)
    deque.addLast(4)
    println(deque) // [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

    println(deque.first()) // 0
    println(deque.last()) // 4

    deque.removeFirst()
    deque.removeLast()
    println(deque) // [1, 2, 3]
}

candidates.text:
Breaking changes and deprecations

To align Kotlin Multiplatform with upcoming changes in Gradle, we are phasing out the withJava() function. Java source sets are now created by default . If you use the Java test fixtures Gradle plugin, upgrade directly to Kotlin 2.1.21 to avoid compatibility issues.

The JetBrains team is proceeding with the deprecation of the kotlin-android-extensions plugin. If you try to use it in your project, you'll now get a configuration error, and no plugin code will be executed.

The legacy kotlin.incremental.classpath.snapshot.enabled property has been removed from the Kotlin Gradle plugin. The property used to provide an opportunity to fall back to a built-in ABI snapshot on the JVM. The plugin now uses other methods to detect and avoid unnecessary recompilations, making the property obsolete.

candidates.text:
Improved JPA support in the kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin

The kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin now automatically applies the all-open compiler plugin with the newly added built-in JPA preset, in addition to applying the existing no-arg compiler plugin.

Previously, using kotlin("plugin.jpa") enabled only the no-arg plugin with JPA presets.

In this release, we improved the kotlin.plugin.jpa preset so the all-open plugin is configured automatically. This ensures that lazy associations work as expected instead of causing eager loading and triggering extra queries.

Starting with Kotlin 2.3.20:

The all-open compiler plugin provides a JPA preset.

The Gradle org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin automatically applies the org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.all-open plugin with the JPA preset enabled.

The Maven JPA setup enables all-open with the JPA preset by default. (Support in IntelliJ IDEA is available from 2026.1.)

The Maven dependency org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-maven-noarg now implicitly includes org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-maven-allopen , so you no longer need to add it explicitly in the <plugin><dependencies> block.

candidates.text:
How to enable

To use named-based destructuring in your project, add the compiler option to your build configuration file:

kotlin {
    compilerOptions {
        freeCompilerArgs.add("-Xname-based-destructuring=only-syntax")
    }
}

<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.jetbrains.kotlin</groupId>
            <artifactId>kotlin-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            <configuration>
                <args>
                    <arg>-Xname-based-destructuring=only-syntax</arg>
                </args>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>

Opting in to name-based destructuring also introduces a new syntax for position-based destructuring using square brackets:

// Uses explicit position-based destructuring
val [username, email] = user

We plan to gradually move toward destructuring declarations using name-based matching by default, while preserving position-based destructuring with the new square bracket syntax.

candidates.text:
Improved JPA support in the kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin

The kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin now automatically applies the all-open compiler plugin with the newly added built-in JPA preset, in addition to applying the existing no-arg compiler plugin.

Previously, using kotlin("plugin.jpa") enabled only the no-arg plugin with JPA presets.

In this release, we improved the kotlin.plugin.jpa preset so the all-open plugin is configured automatically. This ensures that lazy associations work as expected instead of causing eager loading and triggering extra queries.

Starting with Kotlin 2.3.20:

The all-open compiler plugin provides a JPA preset.

The Gradle org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin automatically applies the org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.all-open plugin with the JPA preset enabled.

The Maven JPA setup enables all-open with the JPA preset by default. (Support in IntelliJ IDEA is available from 2026.1.)

The Maven dependency org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-maven-noarg now implicitly includes org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-maven-allopen , so you no longer need to add it explicitly in the <plugin><dependencies> block.

candidates.text:
ArrayDeque

ArrayDeque<T> is an implementation of a double-ended queue, which allows you to add or remove elements both at the beginning or end of the queue. As such, ArrayDeque also fills the role of both a Stack and Queue data structure in Kotlin. Behind the scenes, ArrayDeque is realized using a resizable array that automatically adjusts in size when required:

fun main() {
    val deque = ArrayDeque(listOf(1, 2, 3))

    deque.addFirst(0)
    deque.addLast(4)
    println(deque) // [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

    println(deque.first()) // 0
    println(deque.last()) // 4

    deque.removeFirst()
    deque.removeLast()
    println(deque) // [1, 2, 3]
}

candidates.text:
Breaking changes and deprecations

To align Kotlin Multiplatform with upcoming changes in Gradle, we are phasing out the withJava() function. Java source sets are now created by default . If you use the Java test fixtures Gradle plugin, upgrade directly to Kotlin 2.1.21 to avoid compatibility issues.

The JetBrains team is proceeding with the deprecation of the kotlin-android-extensions plugin. If you try to use it in your project, you'll now get a configuration error, and no plugin code will be executed.

The legacy kotlin.incremental.classpath.snapshot.enabled property has been removed from the Kotlin Gradle plugin. The property used to provide an opportunity to fall back to a built-in ABI snapshot on the JVM. The plugin now uses other methods to detect and avoid unnecessary recompilations, making the property obsolete.

candidates.text:
Following the deprecation of the dead code elimination (DCE) tool used in the legacy Kotlin/JS backend, the remaining DSLs related to DCE are now removed from the Kotlin Gradle plugin:

The org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.dsl.KotlinJsDce interface

The org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.targets.js.dsl.KotlinJsBrowserDsl.dceTask(body: Action<KotlinJsDce>) function

The org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.dsl.KotlinJsDceCompilerToolOptions interface

The org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.dsl.KotlinJsDceOptions interface

The current JS IR compiler supports DCE out of the box, and the @JsExport annotation allows specifying which Kotlin functions and classes to retain during DCE.

candidates.text:
Now, with context-sensitive resolution, you can omit the type name in contexts where the expected type is known:

enum class Problem {
    CONNECTION, AUTHENTICATION, DATABASE, UNKNOWN
}

// Resolves enum entries based on the known type of problem
fun message(problem: Problem): String = when (problem) {
    CONNECTION -> "connection"
    AUTHENTICATION -> "authentication"
    DATABASE -> "database"
    UNKNOWN -> "unknown"
}

The compiler uses this contextual type information to resolve the correct member. This information includes, among other things:

The subject of a when expression

An explicit return type

A declared variable type

Type checks ( is ) and casts ( as )

The known type of a sealed class hierarchy

The declared type of a parameter

candidates.text:
Restrictions for public API inline functions

When an inline function is public or protected but is not a part of a private or internal declaration, it is considered a module 's public API. It can be called in other modules and is inlined at such call sites as well.

This imposes certain risks of binary incompatibility caused by changes in the module that declares an inline function in case the calling module is not re-compiled after the change.

To eliminate the risk of such incompatibility being introduced by a change in a non -public API of a module, public API inline functions are not allowed to use non-public-API declarations, i.e. private and internal declarations and their parts, in their bodies.

An internal declaration can be annotated with @PublishedApi , which allows its use in public API inline functions. When an internal inline function is marked as @PublishedApi , its body is checked too, as if it were public.

chunks.text:
Restrictions for public API inline functions

When an inline function is public or protected but is not a part of a private or internal declaration, it is considered a module 's public API. It can be called in other modules and is inlined at such call sites as well.

This imposes certain risks of binary incompatibility caused by changes in the module that declares an inline function in case the calling module is not re-compiled after the change.

To eliminate the risk of such incompatibility being introduced by a change in a non -public API of a module, public API inline functions are not allowed to use non-public-API declarations, i.e. private and internal declarations and their parts, in their bodies.

An internal declaration can be annotated with @PublishedApi , which allows its use in public API inline functions. When an internal inline function is marked as @PublishedApi , its body is checked too, as if it were public.

Issue : KTLC-384

Component : Core language

Incompatible change type : source

Short summary : Using declarations that implicitly reference inaccessible types from indirect dependencies now results in an error.

To migrate, add an explicit dependency on the module that declares the inaccessible type, or update the intermediate API so it doesn't expose that type.

Deprecation cycle :

2.4.0: raise the warning to an error

candidates.text:
Now, with context-sensitive resolution, you can omit the type name in contexts where the expected type is known:

enum class Problem {
    CONNECTION, AUTHENTICATION, DATABASE, UNKNOWN
}

// Resolves enum entries based on the known type of problem
fun message(problem: Problem): String = when (problem) {
    CONNECTION -> "connection"
    AUTHENTICATION -> "authentication"
    DATABASE -> "database"
    UNKNOWN -> "unknown"
}

The compiler uses this contextual type information to resolve the correct member. This information includes, among other things:

The subject of a when expression

An explicit return type

A declared variable type

Type checks ( is ) and casts ( as )

The known type of a sealed class hierarchy

The declared type of a parameter

Restrictions for public API inline functions

When an inline function is public or protected but is not a part of a private or internal declaration, it is considered a module 's public API. It can be called in other modules and is inlined at such call sites as well.

This imposes certain risks of binary incompatibility caused by changes in the module that declares an inline function in case the calling module is not re-compiled after the change.

To eliminate the risk of such incompatibility being introduced by a change in a non -public API of a module, public API inline functions are not allowed to use non-public-API declarations, i.e. private and internal declarations and their parts, in their bodies.

An internal declaration can be annotated with @PublishedApi , which allows its use in public API inline functions. When an internal inline function is marked as @PublishedApi , its body is checked too, as if it were public.

chunks.text:
Restrictions for public API inline functions

When an inline function is public or protected but is not a part of a private or internal declaration, it is considered a module 's public API. It can be called in other modules and is inlined at such call sites as well.

This imposes certain risks of binary incompatibility caused by changes in the module that declares an inline function in case the calling module is not re-compiled after the change.

To eliminate the risk of such incompatibility being introduced by a change in a non -public API of a module, public API inline functions are not allowed to use non-public-API declarations, i.e. private and internal declarations and their parts, in their bodies.

An internal declaration can be annotated with @PublishedApi , which allows its use in public API inline functions. When an internal inline function is marked as @PublishedApi , its body is checked too, as if it were public.

Rules for expected and actual declarations

To define expected and actual declarations, follow these rules:

In the common source set, declare a standard Kotlin construct. This can be a function, property, class, interface, enumeration, or annotation.

Mark this construct with the expect keyword. This is your expected declaration . These declarations can be used in the common code, but shouldn't include any implementation. Instead, the platform-specific code provides this implementation.

In each platform-specific source set, declare the same construct in the same package and mark it with the actual keyword. This is your actual declaration , which typically contains an implementation using platform-specific libraries.

[2] Expected and actual declarations — Expected and actual declarations > Rules for expected and actual declarations
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-expect-actual.html (normalized source lines 17-27; release unknown; availability unknown)
During compilation for a specific target, the compiler tries to match each actual declaration it finds with the corresponding expected declaration in the common code. The compiler ensures that:

Every expected declaration in the common source set has a matching actual declaration in every platform-specific source set.

Expected declarations don't contain any implementation.

Every actual declaration shares the same package as the corresponding expected declaration, such as org.mygroup.myapp.MyType .

While generating the resulting code for different platforms, the Kotlin compiler merges the expected and actual declarations that correspond to each other. It generates one declaration with its actual implementation for each platform. Every use of the expected declaration in the common code calls the correct actual declaration in the resulting platform code.

You can declare actual declarations when you use intermediate source sets shared between different target platforms. Consider, for example, iosMain as an intermediate source set shared between the iosArm64Main and iosSimulatorArm64Main platform source sets. Only iosMain typically contains the actual declarations and not the platform source sets. The Kotlin compiler will then use these actual declarations to produce the resulting code for the corresponding platforms.

[3] Expected and actual declarations — Expected and actual declarations > Different approaches for using expected and actual declarations > Expected and actual classes > Application in frameworks
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-expect-actual.html (normalized source lines 269-298; release unknown; availability unknown)
Application in frameworks

As a framework author, you can also find expected and actual declarations useful for your framework.

If the example above is part of a framework, the user has to derive a type from CommonIdentity to provide a display name.

In this case, the expected declaration is abstract and declares an abstract method:

// In commonMain of the framework codebase:
expect abstract class CommonIdentity() {
    val userName: String
    val processID: Long
    abstract val displayName: String
}

Similarly, actual implementations are abstract and declare the displayName method:

// In nativeMain of the framework codebase:
actual abstract class CommonIdentity {
    actual val userName = getlogin()?.toKString() ?: "None"
    actual val processID = getpid().toLong()
    actual abstract val displayName: String
}

// In jvmMain of the framework codebase:
actual abstract class CommonIdentity : Identity() {
    actual val userName = login
    actual val processID = pid
    actual abstract val displayName: String
}

[4] Expected and actual declarations — Expected and actual declarations > Different approaches for using expected and actual declarations > Interfaces with expected and actual functions > Expected and actual properties
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-expect-actual.html (normalized source lines 124-152; release unknown; availability unknown)
Expected and actual properties

You can modify the previous example and expect a val property to store an Identity .

Mark this property as expect val and then actualize it in the platform source sets:

//In commonMain source set:
expect val identity: Identity

interface Identity {
    val userName: String
    val processID: Long
}

//In jvmMain source set:
actual val identity: Identity = JVMIdentity()

class JVMIdentity(
    override val userName: String = System.getProperty("user.name") ?: "none",
    override val processID: Long = ProcessHandle.current().pid()
) : Identity

//In nativeMain source set:
actual val identity: Identity = NativeIdentity()

class NativeIdentity(
    override val userName: String = getlogin()?.toKString() ?: "None",
    override val processID: Long = getpid().toLong()
) : Identity

Expected and actual declarations

Expected and actual declarations allow you to access platform-specific APIs from Kotlin Multiplatform modules. You can provide platform-agnostic APIs in the common code.

This article describes the language mechanism of expected and actual declarations. For general recommendations on different ways to use platform-specific APIs, see Use platform-specific APIs .

Expected and actual functions

You can define an Identity type and a factory function buildIdentity() , which is declared in the common source set and implemented differently in platform source sets:

In commonMain , declare a simple type and expect a factory function:

package identity

class Identity(val userName: String, val processID: Long)

expect fun buildIdentity(): Identity

In the jvmMain source set, implement a solution using standard Java libraries:

package identity

import java.lang.System
import java.lang.ProcessHandle

actual fun buildIdentity() = Identity(
    System.getProperty("user.name") ?: "None",
    ProcessHandle.current().pid()
)

candidates.text:
Recommendations on dependency injection

To create a loosely coupled architecture, many Kotlin projects adopt the dependency injection (DI) framework. The DI framework allows injecting dependencies into components based on the current environment.

For example, you might inject different dependencies in testing and in production or when deploying to the cloud compared to hosting locally. As long as a dependency is expressed through an interface, any number of different implementations can be injected, either at compile time or at runtime.

The same principle applies when the dependencies are platform-specific. In the common code, a component can express its dependencies using regular Kotlin interfaces . The DI framework can then be configured to inject a platform-specific implementation, for example, from the JVM or an iOS module.

This means that expected and actual declarations are only needed in the configuration of the DI framework. See Use platform-specific APIs for examples.

Expanded visibility in actual declarations

You can make actual implementations more visible than the corresponding expected declaration. This is useful if you don't want to expose your API as public for common clients.

Currently, the Kotlin compiler issues an error in the case of visibility changes. You can suppress this error by applying @Suppress("ACTUAL_WITHOUT_EXPECT") to the actual type alias declaration. Starting with Kotlin 2.0, this limitation will not apply.

For example, if you declare the following expected declaration in the common source set:

internal expect class Messenger {
    fun sendMessage(message: String)
}

answers.answer:
Expected declarations live in the **common source set** and must be marked with `expect`; they define the API but contain no implementation. Actual declarations live in each **platform-specific source set**, must be marked with `actual`, and provide the implementation. Both must be declared in the **same package** and have **matching signatures** [1][2][5].

Key rules:
- `expect` goes in common code; `actual` goes in platform-specific code [1].
- Every expected declaration must have a matching actual declaration for every platform target [2].
- Expected declarations must not contain any implementation [1][2].
- The package must match (e.g., `org.mygroup.myapp.MyType`) [2].
- Signatures must match; the IDE flags mismatched signatures and package differences [5].

Example:
```kotlin
// commonMain
expect fun platformName(): String

// jvmMain
actual fun platformName(): String = "JVM"

// nativeMain
actual fun platformName(): String = "Native"
```

Note: when using intermediate source sets (e.g., `iosMain` shared by `iosArm64Main` and `iosSimulatorArm64Main`), the `actual` declaration typically lives in the intermediate source set rather than each platform source set [2].

answers.answer:
`expect` declarations go in the **common source set** and `actual` declarations go in each **platform-specific source set**; both must be in the **same package**, and every `expect` declaration must have a matching `actual` for every target [1][2].

Key points:

- In common code, declare a standard Kotlin construct (function, property, class, interface, enum, or annotation) and mark it `expect`; it must not contain an implementation [1][2].
- In each platform source set, declare the same construct *in the same package* and mark it `actual`, providing the implementation [1][2].
- The compiler verifies that every `expect` has a matching `actual` in every platform source set, that `expect` has no implementation, and that packages match [2].
- `actual` declarations may live in an intermediate shared source set (e.g. `iosMain`), and the compiler uses them for the associated platforms [2].

Example:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect fun platformName(): String

// jvmMain
actual fun platformName(): String = "JVM"

// nativeMain
actual fun platformName(): String = "Native"
```

Caveat: The cited guide snapshot does not specify release/version availability, so exact IDE behavior or compiler messaging may vary by version [1][2].

chunks.text:
Rules for expected and actual declarations

To define expected and actual declarations, follow these rules:

In the common source set, declare a standard Kotlin construct. This can be a function, property, class, interface, enumeration, or annotation.

Mark this construct with the expect keyword. This is your expected declaration . These declarations can be used in the common code, but shouldn't include any implementation. Instead, the platform-specific code provides this implementation.

In each platform-specific source set, declare the same construct in the same package and mark it with the actual keyword. This is your actual declaration , which typically contains an implementation using platform-specific libraries.
chunks.title: Expected and actual declarations
sections: Expected and actual declarations > Rules for expected and actual declarations

chunks.text:
During compilation for a specific target, the compiler tries to match each actual declaration it finds with the corresponding expected declaration in the common code. The compiler ensures that:

Every expected declaration in the common source set has a matching actual declaration in every platform-specific source set.

Expected declarations don't contain any implementation.

Every actual declaration shares the same package as the corresponding expected declaration, such as org.mygroup.myapp.MyType .

While generating the resulting code for different platforms, the Kotlin compiler merges the expected and actual declarations that correspond to each other. It generates one declaration with its actual implementation for each platform. Every use of the expected declaration in the common code calls the correct actual declaration in the resulting platform code.

You can declare actual declarations when you use intermediate source sets shared between different target platforms. Consider, for example, iosMain as an intermediate source set shared between the iosArm64Main and iosSimulatorArm64Main platform source sets. Only iosMain typically contains the actual declarations and not the platform source sets. The Kotlin compiler will then use these actual declarations to produce the resulting code for the corresponding platforms.

answers.answer:
`expect` declarations live in a **common source set** (e.g. `commonMain`), while their `actual` counterparts live in each **platform-specific source set** [1]. The same construct must be declared in the **same package** on both sides, and the compiler requires a matching `actual` for every `expect` in every targeted platform source set [1][2]. Expected declarations must not contain any implementation [1][2].

Small example:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect fun platformName(): String

// jvmMain
actual fun platformName(): String = "JVM"

// nativeMain
actual fun platformName(): String = "Native"
```

Version/availability caveat: the cited snapshot has unknown release and availability, so exact behavior may vary by Kotlin version.

Expected and actual declarations

Expected and actual declarations allow you to access platform-specific APIs from Kotlin Multiplatform modules. You can provide platform-agnostic APIs in the common code.

This article describes the language mechanism of expected and actual declarations. For general recommendations on different ways to use platform-specific APIs, see Use platform-specific APIs .

Expected annotation classes

Expected and actual declarations can be used with annotations. For example, you can declare an @XmlSerializable annotation, which must have a corresponding actual declaration in each platform source set:

@Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS)
@Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME)
expect annotation class XmlSerializable()

@XmlSerializable
class Person(val name: String, val age: Int)

It might be helpful to reuse existing types on a particular platform. For example, on the JVM, you can define your annotation using the existing type from the JAXB specification :

import javax.xml.bind.annotation.XmlRootElement

actual typealias XmlSerializable = XmlRootElement

Expected and actual classes

Expected and actual classes are in Beta . They are almost stable, but migration steps may be required in the future. We'll do our best to minimize any further changes for you to make.

You can use expected and actual classes to implement the same solution:

// In the commonMain source set:
expect class Identity() {
    val userName: String
    val processID: Int
}

// In the jvmMain source set:
actual class Identity {
    actual val userName: String = System.getProperty("user.name") ?: "None"
    actual val processID: Long = ProcessHandle.current().pid()
}

// In the nativeMain source set:
actual class Identity {
    actual val userName: String = getlogin()?.toKString() ?: "None"
    actual val processID: Long = getpid().toLong()
}

candidates.text:
Recommendations on dependency injection

To create a loosely coupled architecture, many Kotlin projects adopt the dependency injection (DI) framework. The DI framework allows injecting dependencies into components based on the current environment.

For example, you might inject different dependencies in testing and in production or when deploying to the cloud compared to hosting locally. As long as a dependency is expressed through an interface, any number of different implementations can be injected, either at compile time or at runtime.

The same principle applies when the dependencies are platform-specific. In the common code, a component can express its dependencies using regular Kotlin interfaces . The DI framework can then be configured to inject a platform-specific implementation, for example, from the JVM or an iOS module.

This means that expected and actual declarations are only needed in the configuration of the DI framework. See Use platform-specific APIs for examples.

You can make actual implementations more visible than the corresponding expected declaration. This is useful if you don't want to expose your API as public for common clients.

internal expect class Messenger {
    fun sendMessage(message: String)
}

answers.answer:
**Where they live:** the `expect` declaration goes in the **common source set**; the `actual` declarations go in **each platform-specific source set** (or an intermediate shared source set such as `iosMain`) [1][2].

**What must match:** the compiler matches each actual to its expected and requires that:

- Every `expect` declaration in common has a matching `actual` in every platform-specific source set [2].
- Both share the **same package** (e.g. `org.mygroup.myapp.MyType`) [1][2].
- The expected declaration contains **no implementation** [1][2].

The compiler then merges the pair per platform, so common-code uses of the expected declaration resolve to the platform's actual implementation [2].

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect fun platformName(): String

// jvmMain
actual fun platformName(): String = System.getProperty("os.name") ?: "Unknown"
```

Version caveat: expect/actual classes are documented as Beta [5]; the other cited rules carry no release/availability guarantee.

Using type aliases to satisfy actual declarations

The implementation of an actual declaration does not have to be written from scratch. It can be an existing type, such as a class provided by a third-party library.

You can use this type as long as it meets all the requirements associated with the expected declaration. For example, consider these two expected declarations:

expect enum class Month {
    JANUARY, FEBRUARY, MARCH, APRIL, MAY, JUNE, JULY,
    AUGUST, SEPTEMBER, OCTOBER, NOVEMBER, DECEMBER
}

expect class MyDate {
    fun getYear(): Int
    fun getMonth(): Month
    fun getDayOfMonth(): Int
}

Within a JVM module, the java.time.Month enum can be used to implement the first expected declaration and the java.time.LocalDate class to implement the second. However, there's no way to add the actual keyword directly to these types.

Expected and actual properties

You can modify the previous example and expect a val property to store an Identity .

Mark this property as expect val and then actualize it in the platform source sets:

//In commonMain source set:
expect val identity: Identity

interface Identity {
    val userName: String
    val processID: Long
}

//In jvmMain source set:
actual val identity: Identity = JVMIdentity()

class JVMIdentity(
    override val userName: String = System.getProperty("user.name") ?: "none",
    override val processID: Long = ProcessHandle.current().pid()
) : Identity

//In nativeMain source set:
actual val identity: Identity = NativeIdentity()

class NativeIdentity(
    override val userName: String = getlogin()?.toKString() ?: "None",
    override val processID: Long = getpid().toLong()
) : Identity

chunks.text:
Rules for expected and actual declarations

To define expected and actual declarations, follow these rules:

In the common source set, declare a standard Kotlin construct. This can be a function, property, class, interface, enumeration, or annotation.

Mark this construct with the expect keyword. This is your expected declaration . These declarations can be used in the common code, but shouldn't include any implementation. Instead, the platform-specific code provides this implementation.

In each platform-specific source set, declare the same construct in the same package and mark it with the actual keyword. This is your actual declaration , which typically contains an implementation using platform-specific libraries.
chunks.title: Expected and actual declarations
sections: Expected and actual declarations > Rules for expected and actual declarations

chunks.text:
During compilation for a specific target, the compiler tries to match each actual declaration it finds with the corresponding expected declaration in the common code. The compiler ensures that:

Every expected declaration in the common source set has a matching actual declaration in every platform-specific source set.

Expected declarations don't contain any implementation.

Every actual declaration shares the same package as the corresponding expected declaration, such as org.mygroup.myapp.MyType .

While generating the resulting code for different platforms, the Kotlin compiler merges the expected and actual declarations that correspond to each other. It generates one declaration with its actual implementation for each platform. Every use of the expected declaration in the common code calls the correct actual declaration in the resulting platform code.

You can declare actual declarations when you use intermediate source sets shared between different target platforms. Consider, for example, iosMain as an intermediate source set shared between the iosArm64Main and iosSimulatorArm64Main platform source sets. Only iosMain typically contains the actual declarations and not the platform source sets. The Kotlin compiler will then use these actual declarations to produce the resulting code for the corresponding platforms.

answers.answer:
**Where they live:**
- The `expect` declaration goes in the **common source set** (e.g. `commonMain`), marked with `expect`, with no implementation [1].
- The `actual` declaration goes in each **platform-specific source set** (e.g. `jvmMain`, `nativeMain`), marked with `actual`, and typically provides the platform-specific implementation [1].
- For intermediate source sets shared across targets (e.g. `iosMain` shared by `iosArm64Main` and `iosSimulatorArm64Main`), the `actual` declarations are typically placed in the intermediate source set rather than in each platform source set [2].

**What must match:**
- Every `expect` declaration must have a matching `actual` declaration in **every** platform-specific source set [2].
- They must be in the **same package** (e.g. `org.mygroup.myapp.MyType`) [2].
- The `expect` declaration must not contain any implementation [2].

**Example:**
```kotlin
// commonMain
expect val identity: Identity

interface Identity {
    val userName: String
    val processID: Long
}
```
```kotlin
// jvmMain
actual val identity: Identity = JVMIdentity()

class JVMIdentity(
    override val userName: String = System.getProperty("user.name") ?: "none",
    override val processID: Long = ProcessHandle.current().pid()
) : Identity
```
[4]

**Note:** An `actual` declaration doesn't have to be written from scratch — it can be satisfied by an existing type (including via a type alias), as long as it meets the requirements of the `expect` declaration [3].

The snapshot doesn't state which Kotlin version introduced these rules, so version-specific behavior isn't guaranteed beyond the cited documentation.

candidates.text:
Recommendations on dependency injection

To create a loosely coupled architecture, many Kotlin projects adopt the dependency injection (DI) framework. The DI framework allows injecting dependencies into components based on the current environment.

For example, you might inject different dependencies in testing and in production or when deploying to the cloud compared to hosting locally. As long as a dependency is expressed through an interface, any number of different implementations can be injected, either at compile time or at runtime.

The same principle applies when the dependencies are platform-specific. In the common code, a component can express its dependencies using regular Kotlin interfaces . The DI framework can then be configured to inject a platform-specific implementation, for example, from the JVM or an iOS module.

This means that expected and actual declarations are only needed in the configuration of the DI framework. See Use platform-specific APIs for examples.

answers.answer:
# Where `expect`/`actual` Declarations Live and What Must Match

## Placement

- **`expect` declarations** go in the **common source set** and are marked with the `expect` keyword. They are standard Kotlin constructs (function, property, class, interface, enum, or annotation) with **no implementation** [1].
- **`actual` declarations** go in each **platform-specific source set**, marked with `actual`, and typically provide a platform-specific implementation [1]. They may also be placed in **intermediate source sets** shared between targets (e.g., `iosMain` shared by `iosArm64Main` and `iosSimulatorArm64Main`) [2].

## What must match

During compilation for a specific target, the compiler matches each `actual` with its corresponding `expect` and enforces [2]:

1. **Every** `expect` in the common source set has a matching `actual` in **every** platform-specific source set.
2. `expect` declarations contain **no implementation**.
3. The `actual` shares the **same package** as the corresponding `expect` (e.g., `org.mygroup.myapp.MyType`).

## Merging

The compiler merges matching `expect`/`actual` pairs, generating one declaration with the `actual` implementation for each platform. Uses of the `expect` declaration in common code resolve to the correct `actual` in the resulting platform code [2].

## Type-alias caveat

An `actual` doesn't have to be written from scratch — it can be satisfied by an existing type (e.g., a third-party class) via a type alias, provided that type meets all requirements of the `expect` declaration [3].

## Example

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect val identity: Identity

interface Identity {
    val userName: String
    val processID: Long
}

// jvmMain
actual val identity: Identity = JVMIdentity()

// nativeMain
actual val identity: Identity = NativeIdentity()
```

Here the `expect val` lives in `commonMain` and each `actual val` provides a platform-specific value [4].

## Version caveat

The snapshot cites no release and marks availability as unknown; **release versions are not feature availability**, so verify these rules against the docs for your specific Kotlin version [1][2].

answers.answer:
**Where they live:** The `expect` declaration goes in the **common source set**, and the corresponding `actual` declaration goes in **each platform-specific source set** [1]. Actuals can also be declared in an **intermediate source set** shared between targets (e.g. `iosMain` for `iosArm64Main` and `iosSimulatorArm64Main`); the compiler then uses those actuals for the corresponding platforms [2].

**What must match:**

- **Package** — every actual must share the same package as its expected declaration (e.g. `org.mygroup.myapp.MyType`) [1][2].
- **Construct kind and signature** — the expected construct can be a function, property, class, interface, enum, or annotation, and the actual must match it [1].
- **No implementation in the expected declaration** — it must not contain a body/implementation [1][2].
- **Coverage** — every expected declaration must have a matching actual in *every* platform-specific source set being compiled [2].

The compiler matches each actual to its expected during target compilation; if both rules are satisfied, it merges them into one declaration using the platform implementation, so common-code uses of the expected call the correct actual [2].

Example:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect fun platformName(): String

// jvmMain
actual fun platformName(): String = "JVM"

// nativeMain
actual fun platformName(): String = "Native"
```

If the implementation already exists as another type, you can satisfy the actual using a **type alias** instead of writing it from scratch, provided the type meets the expected declaration's requirements (e.g. `java.time.Month` for an expected `Month` enum) [3].

One caveat: intermediate source sets are a more advanced pattern; the docs present them as an available option for shared actuals, not as the default structure [2].

It generates one declaration with its actual implementation for each platform. Every use of the expected declaration in the common code calls the correct actual declaration in the resulting platform code.

You can declare actual declarations when you use intermediate source sets shared between different target platforms. Consider, for example, iosMain as an intermediate source set shared between the iosArm64Main and iosSimulatorArm64Main platform source sets. Only iosMain typically contains the actual declarations and not the platform source sets. The Kotlin compiler will then use these actual declarations to produce the resulting code for the corresponding platforms.

Expected and actual declarations allow you to access platform-specific APIs from Kotlin Multiplatform modules. You can provide platform-agnostic APIs in the common code.

Expected declarations live in a **common source set** and are marked with `expect`; each actual declaration lives in a **platform-specific source set** (or a shared intermediate source set) and is marked with `actual` [1][2]. During compilation, the compiler matches each `actual` with its corresponding `expect` for a specific target [2].

Required to match:
- Same construct kind (function, property, class, interface, enum, or annotation) [1]
- Same **package**, e.g. `org.mygroup.myapp.MyType` [2]
- Every `expect` must have a matching `actual` in every platform source set, and the `expect` must not contain any implementation [1][2]

Example:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect fun platformName(): String

// jvmMain
actual fun platformName(): String = System.getProperty("os.name") ?: "Unknown"
```

answers.answer:
Yes. There are two main approaches:

## 1. Type aliases (most direct)

An `actual typealias` maps the expected declaration directly to an existing platform type:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect class MyDate

// jvmMain
actual typealias MyDate = java.time.LocalDate
```

The alias must be declared in the same package as the expected declaration, and the referred class lives elsewhere [2]. If the platform type references other types (e.g. `LocalDate` uses `Month`), those must also be declared as `expect`/`actual` — hence the doc's example declares both `Month` and `MyDate` [2].

## 2. Inheriting from the platform class

You can also make an `actual class` extend an existing platform base class, exposing its members as `actual` properties:

```kotlin
// jvmMain
actual class CommonIdentity : Identity() {
    actual val userName = login
    actual val processID = pid
}
```

Here `CommonIdentity` is compatible with your common design while taking advantage of the existing platform type [1].

## Caveats

- `typealias` cannot be used to satisfy an `expect` if the aliased platform type doesn't match the expected shape (e.g. same-enum constants — extra entries are allowed on actualization but the expected constants must all be present) [5].
- Visibility expansion (e.g. an `internal` expect satisfied by a `public` platform type) requires `@Suppress("ACTUAL_WITHOUT_EXPECT")` on the `actual typealias` [3].
- The reference material is version-agnostic; confirm exact rules against your Kotlin release.

answers.answer:
Yes — in Kotlin Multiplatform you can satisfy a common `expect class` with an existing platform type instead of manually wrapping it, using one of these approaches:

**1. Inherit from the platform class in the actual declaration**

If the platform type already exists (e.g. `Identity` on the JVM), your `actual class` can extend it and expose the expected members:

```kotlin
// jvmMain
actual class CommonIdentity : Identity() {
    actual val userName = login
    actual val processID = pid
}
```

The docs describe exactly this pattern for reusing existing platform classes while keeping a common API [1][2].

**2. Use a typealias in the actual declaration**

For expected types whose platform counterpart is a plain class, you can map the `expect` directly to the platform type:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect class MyDate

// jvmMain (in the same package as the expectation)
actual typealias MyDate = java.time.LocalDate
```

The typealias must be declared in the same package as the expected declaration, and the referred class is defined elsewhere [4]. You can also use typealiases to expose an existing public class as the actual for an internal expected class with `@Suppress("ACTUAL_WITHOUT_EXPECT")` [3].

Caveat: exact keyword combinations (`expect class` + `actual typealias`, inheritance rules, suppression behavior) can differ across compiler versions, and the reference snapshots don't pin a release or availability, so verify against the Kotlin version you're using.

expect enum class Month {

Caveat: the alias target must be a real type you can reference; you cannot attach `actual` directly to a third-party or JDK type. [2]

answers.answer:
Yes. On each platform where that specific `actual` is required, you can satisfy an expected class with an existing platform type by using an `actual typealias`, instead of wrapping the platform type in a new class.

The platform type must meet the requirements of the expected declaration, and the typealias should be in the same package as the expected declaration; the referred class can be defined elsewhere. [1] This is exactly the documented use case for reusing a third-party class as an `actual` declaration, since you cannot add the `actual` keyword directly to an existing type. [3]

Example:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect class MyDate {
    fun getYear(): Int
    fun getMonth(): Month
    fun getDayOfMonth(): Int
}

expect enum class Month {
    JANUARY, FEBRUARY, MARCH, APRIL, MAY, JUNE, JULY,
    AUGUST, SEPTEMBER, OCTOBER, NOVEMBER, DECEMBER
}
```

```kotlin
// jvmMain
actual typealias Month = java.time.Month
actual typealias MyDate = java.time.LocalDate
```

Note that if the platform type depends on another expected type, that dependency also needs an expected declaration in common code. For example, because `LocalDate` uses `Month`, both need expected classes. [1]

The same pattern can also be used for expected annotation classes, e.g. `actual typealias XmlSerializable = XmlRootElement`. [4]

Caveat: the references do not specify which Kotlin versions support these behaviors; availability may vary.

You can use this type as long as it meets all the requirements associated with the expected declaration. For example, consider these two expected declarations:

expect enum class Month {
    JANUARY, FEBRUARY, MARCH, APRIL, MAY, JUNE, JULY,
    AUGUST, SEPTEMBER, OCTOBER, NOVEMBER, DECEMBER

answers.answer:
Yes, in Kotlin Multiplatform you can satisfy an `expect` declaration with an existing platform type by using an `actual typealias` rather than wrapping it in a new class. This works when the existing type already meets all the requirements of the expected declaration [1][2].

**Example** — matching a platform date type:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect enum class Month {
    JANUARY, FEBRUARY, /* ... */
}
expect class MyDate {
    fun getYear(): Int
    fun getMonth(): Month
    fun getDayOfMonth(): Int
}

// jvmMain
actual typealias Month = java.time.Month
actual typealias MyDate = java.time.LocalDate
```

Constraints to keep in mind:

- The `actual typealias` must be declared in the **same package** as the expected declaration, and the referred class must be defined elsewhere [1].
- The platform type must satisfy the expected declaration's API. For example, because `LocalDate` uses `Month`, you also need an expected declaration for `Month` (as shown above) [1].
- You can't add the `actual` keyword directly to a third-party or JDK type; a typealias is the mechanism for reusing it [2].
- This also works for `expect annotation class`: you can satisfy it with `actual typealias` pointing to an existing annotation type, e.g. `actual typealias XmlSerializable = XmlRootElement` [3].

If the expected declaration is a function or something that must be *created*, an interface-based approach (a common interface with platform-specific implementations) may be more appropriate [4].

**Caveat:** The referenced snapshots don't state a Kotlin release version, so exact behavior and availability of `expect`/`actual typealias` may vary across versions.

candidates.text:
Different approaches for using expected and actual declarations

Let's explore the different options of using the expect/actual mechanism to solve the problem of accessing platform APIs while still providing a way to work with them in the common code.

Consider a Kotlin Multiplatform project where you need to implement the Identity type, which should contain the user's login name and the current process ID. The project has the commonMain , jvmMain , and nativeMain source sets to make the application work on the JVM and in native environments like iOS.

candidates.text:
Expected and actual functions

You can define an Identity type and a factory function buildIdentity() , which is declared in the common source set and implemented differently in platform source sets:

In commonMain , declare a simple type and expect a factory function:

package identity

class Identity(val userName: String, val processID: Long)

expect fun buildIdentity(): Identity

In the jvmMain source set, implement a solution using standard Java libraries:

package identity

import java.lang.System
import java.lang.ProcessHandle

actual fun buildIdentity() = Identity(
    System.getProperty("user.name") ?: "None",
    ProcessHandle.current().pid()
)

candidates.text:
Rules for expected and actual declarations

To define expected and actual declarations, follow these rules:

In the common source set, declare a standard Kotlin construct. This can be a function, property, class, interface, enumeration, or annotation.

Mark this construct with the expect keyword. This is your expected declaration . These declarations can be used in the common code, but shouldn't include any implementation. Instead, the platform-specific code provides this implementation.

In each platform-specific source set, declare the same construct in the same package and mark it with the actual keyword. This is your actual declaration , which typically contains an implementation using platform-specific libraries.

answers.answer:
Yes, in Kotlin Multiplatform you can satisfy a common `expected` class using an existing platform type, but the mechanism depends on the case.

Two documented approaches:

**1. Inherit from the platform class**

If the platform type is a class you can extend, declare an `actual class` that inherits from it and maps its members:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect class CommonIdentity() {
    val userName: String
    val processID: Long
}

// jvmMain
actual class CommonIdentity : Identity() {
    actual val userName = login
    actual val processID = pid
}
```

The expected `CommonIdentity` is compatible with your design while reusing the existing JVM `Identity` type [1][2].

**2. Use a type alias (no wrapping)**

If you don't need to extend anything and the platform type already has the right shape, a `typealias` can connect the expected declaration directly to the platform type — no wrapper class is generated:

```kotlin
// commonMain
expect class MyDate(...)  // or expect enum class Month

// jvmMain
actual typealias Month = java.time.Month
actual typealias MyDate = java.time.LocalDate
```

The typealias must be declared in the same package as the expected declaration; the referred class can live elsewhere [3]. Type aliases can also expand visibility (e.g., an internal expected class aliased to an existing public type) [4].

Caveats:
- The general guidance is to prefer interfaces or standard constructs over `expect`/`actual` classes when sufficient; expected/actual classes are in Beta and the compiler emits a warning unless you opt in with `-Xexpect-actual-classes` [5].
- A typealias only works when the platform type's API matches the expected declaration's contract; otherwise you still need an actual class (possibly inheriting from the platform type).

The reference snapshot doesn't state version availability, so exact behavior/compiler flags may vary by release.

Using type aliases to satisfy actual declarations

The implementation of an actual declaration does not have to be written from scratch. It can be an existing type, such as a class provided by a third-party library.

You can use this type as long as it meets all the requirements associated with the expected declaration. For example, consider these two expected declarations:

expect enum class Month {
    JANUARY, FEBRUARY, MARCH, APRIL, MAY, JUNE, JULY,
    AUGUST, SEPTEMBER, OCTOBER, NOVEMBER, DECEMBER
}

expect class MyDate {
    fun getYear(): Int
    fun getMonth(): Month
    fun getDayOfMonth(): Int
}

Within a JVM module, the java.time.Month enum can be used to implement the first expected declaration and the java.time.LocalDate class to implement the second. However, there's no way to add the actual keyword directly to these types.

[4] Expected and actual declarations — Expected and actual declarations > Advanced use cases > Expected annotation classes
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/multiplatform/multiplatform-expect-actual.html (normalized source lines 389-404; release unknown; availability unknown)
Expected annotation classes

Expected and actual declarations can be used with annotations. For example, you can declare an @XmlSerializable annotation, which must have a corresponding actual declaration in each platform source set:

@Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS)
@Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME)
expect annotation class XmlSerializable()

@XmlSerializable
class Person(val name: String, val age: Int)

It might be helpful to reuse existing types on a particular platform. For example, on the JVM, you can define your annotation using the existing type from the JAXB specification :

import javax.xml.bind.annotation.XmlRootElement

actual typealias XmlSerializable = XmlRootElement

actual class CommonIdentity {
    actual val userName = getlogin()?.toKString() ?: "None"

In jvmMain , provide an actual declaration that inherits from the platform-specific base class:

answers.answer:
Yes. In Kotlin Multiplatform, an `actual` declaration can be satisfied with an existing platform type via an `actual typealias`, as long as the aliased type meets all the requirements of the `expect` declaration.

For example, given a common expected class:

```kotlin
expect class MyDate {
    fun getYear(): Int
    fun getMonth(): Month
    fun getDayOfMonth(): Int
}
```

You can satisfy it on the JVM with an existing `java.time.LocalDate` using a type alias:

```kotlin
actual typealias MyDate = java.time.LocalDate
```

The type alias must be declared in the same package as the expected declaration, and the referred class should be created elsewhere [1]. If the expected type depends on other expected types (e.g., `Month`), those also need matching `actual` declarations (which can themselves be type aliases) [1].

You can even expand visibility: an `internal` expected class can be satisfied with an existing `public` type via `actual typealias`, adding `@Suppress("ACTUAL_WITHOUT_EXPECT")` as needed [2].

This approach avoids writing a wrapper class from scratch and lets you reuse existing platform (or third-party) types [3].

[1] Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C — Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C > Mappings > Errors and exceptions
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-objc-interop.html (normalized source lines 218-228; release unknown; availability unknown)
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.
How are Kotlin exceptions exposed to Swift and Objective-C callers?

candidates.text:
Hide Kotlin declarations from Objective-C and Swift

To make your Kotlin code more Swift/Objective-C-friendly, use the @HiddenFromObjC annotation to hide a Kotlin declaration from Objective-C and Swift. It disables the function or property export to Objective-C.

Alternatively, you can mark Kotlin declarations with the internal modifier to restrict their visibility in the compilation module. Use @HiddenFromObjC if you want to hide the Kotlin declaration from Objective-C and Swift while keeping it visible to other Kotlin modules.

See an example in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

candidates.text:
Extensions and category members

Members of Objective-C categories and Swift extensions are generally imported to Kotlin as extensions. That's why these declarations can't be overridden in Kotlin, and the extension initializers aren't available as Kotlin constructors.

Currently, there are two exceptions. Starting with Kotlin 1.8.20, category members that are declared in the same headers as the NSView class (from the AppKit framework) or UIView classes (from the UIKit framework) are imported as members of these classes. This means that you can override methods that subclass from NSView or UIView.

Kotlin extensions to "regular" Kotlin classes are imported to Swift and Objective-C as extensions and category members, respectively. Kotlin extensions to other types are treated as top-level declarations with an additional receiver parameter. These types include:

candidates.text:
Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C

The Objective-C libraries import is in Beta . All Kotlin declarations generated by the cinterop tool from Objective-C libraries should have the @ExperimentalForeignApi annotation.

Native platform libraries shipped with Kotlin/Native (like Foundation, UIKit, and POSIX) require opt-in only for some APIs.

Kotlin/Native provides indirect interoperability with Swift through Objective-C. This document covers how you can use Kotlin declarations in Swift/Objective-C code and Objective-C declarations in Kotlin code.

Some other resources you might find useful:

The Kotlin-Swift interopedia , a collection of examples on how to use Kotlin declarations in Swift code.

Importing Swift/Objective-C libraries to Kotlin

Objective-C frameworks and libraries can be used in Kotlin code if properly imported to the build (system frameworks are imported by default). For more details, see:

Create and configure a library definition file

Configure compilation for native libraries

A Swift library can be used in Kotlin code if its API is exported to Objective-C with @objc . Pure Swift modules are not yet supported.

candidates.text:
Initializers

A Swift/Objective-C initializer is imported to Kotlin as constructors or as factory methods named create . The latter happens with initializers declared in the Objective-C category or as a Swift extension, because Kotlin has no concept of extension constructors.

Before importing Swift initializers to Kotlin, don't forget to annotate them with @objc .

Kotlin constructors are imported as initializers to Swift/Objective-C.

Unsupported

Some features of the Kotlin programming language are not yet mapped into the respective features of Objective-C or Swift. Currently, the following features are not properly exposed in generated framework headers:

Inline classes (arguments are mapped as either underlying primitive type or id )

Custom classes implementing standard Kotlin collection interfaces ( List , Map , Set ) and other special classes

Kotlin subclasses of Objective-C classes

candidates.text:
Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

Concurrency support . You can seamlessly call suspending Kotlin code from Swift and export kotlinx.coroutines flows as Swift's AsyncSequence out of the box.

candidates.text:
Method names translation

Generally, Swift argument labels and Objective-C selector pieces are mapped to Kotlin parameter names. These two concepts have different semantics, so sometimes Swift/Objective-C methods can be imported with a clashing Kotlin signature. In this case, the clashing methods can be called from Kotlin using named arguments, for example:

[player moveTo:LEFT byMeters:17]
[player moveTo:UP byInches:42]

In Kotlin, it's:

player.moveTo(LEFT, byMeters = 17)
player.moveTo(UP, byInches = 42)

Here's how the kotlin.Any functions are mapped to Swift/Objective-C:

Kotlin | Swift | Objective-C
equals() | isEquals(_:) | isEquals:
hashCode() | hash | hash
toString() | description | description

candidates.text:
Interoperability with Swift using Swift export

Kotlin's interoperability with Swift through Swift export is currently in Alpha. Swift export allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

Swift export makes multiplatform development for Apple targets more streamlined. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

Current Swift export features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

candidates.text:
Swift export available by default

Kotlin 2.2.20 introduces experimental support for Swift export. It allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

This should significantly improve multiplatform development for Apple targets. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

The key features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

evidence.query: How are Kotlin exceptions exposed to Swift and Objective-C callers?

chunks.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.

answers.answer:
Kotlin exceptions are exposed to Swift/Objective-C via the `@Throws` annotation:

- All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, while Swift only has checked errors handled at compile time. So if Swift/Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with `@Throws`, listing the "expected" exception classes [1].
- When compiling to a Swift/Objective-C framework, non-`suspend` functions that have or inherit `@Throws` become `NSError*`-producing methods in Objective-C and `throws` methods in Swift. `suspend` functions always have an `NSError*`/`Error` parameter in the completion handler [1].
- If a called Kotlin function throws an exception that is an instance of a class specified in `@Throws` (or a subclass), the exception is propagated as an `NSError`. Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination [1].
- `suspend` functions without `@Throws` propagate only `CancellationException` (as `NSError`). Non-`suspend` functions without `@Throws` don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all [1].

Note: the reverse direction is not implemented yet — Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing [1].

candidates.text:
Method names translation

Generally, Swift argument labels and Objective-C selector pieces are mapped to Kotlin parameter names. These two concepts have different semantics, so sometimes Swift/Objective-C methods can be imported with a clashing Kotlin signature. In this case, the clashing methods can be called from Kotlin using named arguments, for example:

[player moveTo:LEFT byMeters:17]
[player moveTo:UP byInches:42]

In Kotlin, it's:

player.moveTo(LEFT, byMeters = 17)
player.moveTo(UP, byInches = 42)

Here's how the kotlin.Any functions are mapped to Swift/Objective-C:

Kotlin | Swift | Objective-C
equals() | isEquals(_:) | isEquals:
hashCode() | hash | hash
toString() | description | description

See an example with data classes in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

chunks.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.

answers.answer:
Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, but Swift only has checked errors. To bridge them, mark Kotlin functions that throw with `@Throws(...)`.

- A non-`suspend` function with/inheriting `@Throws` is exposed to Objective-C as an `NSError*`-producing method and to Swift as a `throws` method [1].
- If a thrown exception is one of the classes listed in `@Throws` or a subclass, it propagates as `NSError` [1].
- Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are unhandled and cause program termination [1].
- `suspend` functions always expose an `NSError*`/`Error` parameter in the completion handler; without `@Throws`, they propagate only `CancellationException` as `NSError` [1].
- Non-`suspend` functions without `@Throws` don’t propagate Kotlin exceptions at all [1].
- Reverse direction isn’t implemented: Swift/Objective-C throwing methods aren’t imported into Kotlin as exception-throwing [1].
