The Objective-C libraries import is in Beta . All Kotlin declarations generated by the cinterop tool from Objective-C libraries should have the @ExperimentalForeignApi annotation.

Native platform libraries shipped with Kotlin/Native (like Foundation, UIKit, and POSIX) require opt-in only for some APIs.

Hide Kotlin declarations from Objective-C and Swift

To make your Kotlin code more Swift/Objective-C-friendly, use the @HiddenFromObjC annotation to hide a Kotlin declaration from Objective-C and Swift. It disables the function or property export to Objective-C.

candidates.text:
Method names translation

Generally, Swift argument labels and Objective-C selector pieces are mapped to Kotlin parameter names. These two concepts have different semantics, so sometimes Swift/Objective-C methods can be imported with a clashing Kotlin signature. In this case, the clashing methods can be called from Kotlin using named arguments, for example:

[player moveTo:LEFT byMeters:17]
[player moveTo:UP byInches:42]

In Kotlin, it's:

player.moveTo(LEFT, byMeters = 17)
player.moveTo(UP, byInches = 42)

Here's how the kotlin.Any functions are mapped to Swift/Objective-C:

Kotlin | Swift | Objective-C
equals() | isEquals(_:) | isEquals:
hashCode() | hash | hash
toString() | description | description

See an example with data classes in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

Swift export available by default

Kotlin 2.2.20 introduces experimental support for Swift export. It allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

This should significantly improve multiplatform development for Apple targets. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

answers.answer:
Kotlin exceptions are **unchecked** — normally they are not exposed as declared errors to Swift/Objective-C [1]. To make a Kotlin function callable as a throwing method from Swift/Objective-C, you must mark it with `@Throws`, listing the expected exception classes [1].

Key points:

- Non-`suspend` functions with (or inheriting) `@Throws` become `NSError*`-producing methods in Objective-C and `throws` methods in Swift [1].
- `suspend` functions always have an `NSError*` / `Error` parameter in the completion handler [1].
- If a thrown exception is an instance of a class listed in `@Throws` (or a subclass), it propagates as `NSError`; other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are unhandled and cause program termination [1].
- `suspend` functions without `@Throws` propagate only `CancellationException` (as `NSError`); non-`suspend` functions without `@Throws` do not propagate Kotlin exceptions at all [1].
- The reverse direction is not implemented: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods are not imported into Kotlin as exception-throwing [1].

Example:

```kotlin
@Throws(IOException::class)
fun writeToFile() {
    throw IOException()
}
```

For Java callers, the same annotation is needed so Java signatures declare the checked exception [3]. Note that this is Kotlin/Native indirect interoperability with Swift through Objective-C [4].

Kotlin extensions to "regular" Kotlin classes are imported to Swift and Objective-C as extensions and category members, respectively. Kotlin extensions to other types are treated as top-level declarations with an additional receiver parameter. These types include:

Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C

The Objective-C libraries import is in Beta . All Kotlin declarations generated by the cinterop tool from Objective-C libraries should have the @ExperimentalForeignApi annotation.

Native platform libraries shipped with Kotlin/Native (like Foundation, UIKit, and POSIX) require opt-in only for some APIs.

Kotlin/Native provides indirect interoperability with Swift through Objective-C. This document covers how you can use Kotlin declarations in Swift/Objective-C code and Objective-C declarations in Kotlin code.

candidates.text:
Hide Kotlin declarations from Objective-C and Swift

To make your Kotlin code more Swift/Objective-C-friendly, use the @HiddenFromObjC annotation to hide a Kotlin declaration from Objective-C and Swift. It disables the function or property export to Objective-C.

Alternatively, you can mark Kotlin declarations with the internal modifier to restrict their visibility in the compilation module. Use @HiddenFromObjC if you want to hide the Kotlin declaration from Objective-C and Swift while keeping it visible to other Kotlin modules.

See an example in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

A Swift/Objective-C initializer is imported to Kotlin as constructors or as factory methods named create . The latter happens with initializers declared in the Objective-C category or as a Swift extension, because Kotlin has no concept of extension constructors.

candidates.text:
Method names translation

Generally, Swift argument labels and Objective-C selector pieces are mapped to Kotlin parameter names. These two concepts have different semantics, so sometimes Swift/Objective-C methods can be imported with a clashing Kotlin signature. In this case, the clashing methods can be called from Kotlin using named arguments, for example:

[player moveTo:LEFT byMeters:17]
[player moveTo:UP byInches:42]

In Kotlin, it's:

player.moveTo(LEFT, byMeters = 17)
player.moveTo(UP, byInches = 42)

Here's how the kotlin.Any functions are mapped to Swift/Objective-C:

Kotlin | Swift | Objective-C
equals() | isEquals(_:) | isEquals:
hashCode() | hash | hash
toString() | description | description

See an example with data classes in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

Concurrency support . You can seamlessly call suspending Kotlin code from Swift and export kotlinx.coroutines flows as Swift's AsyncSequence out of the box.

candidates.text:
Swift export available by default

Kotlin 2.2.20 introduces experimental support for Swift export. It allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

This should significantly improve multiplatform development for Apple targets. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

The key features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

Swift/Objective-C collections are mapped to Kotlin as described in the mappings table , except for NSMutableSet and NSMutableDictionary .

NSMutableSet isn't converted to a Kotlin's MutableSet . To pass an object to Kotlin MutableSet , explicitly create this kind of Kotlin collection. candidates.text:
The overriding constructor must have the same parameter names and types as the overridden one.

To override different methods with clashing Kotlin signatures, you can add the @ObjCSignatureOverride annotation to the class. The annotation instructs the Kotlin compiler to ignore conflicting overloads, in case several functions with the same argument types, but different argument names, are inherited from the Objective-C class.

By default, the Kotlin/Native compiler doesn't allow calling a non-designated Objective-C initializer as a super() constructor. This behavior can be inconvenient if the designated initializers aren't marked properly in the Objective-C library. To disable these compiler checks, add the disableDesignatedInitializerChecks = true to the library's .def file .

evidence.query: How are Kotlin exceptions exposed to Swift and Objective-C callers?

chunks.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.
chunks.title: Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C
sections: Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C > Mappings > Errors and exceptions

answers.answer:
Kotlin exceptions are exposed to Swift/Objective-C callers via the `@Throws` annotation, but with important limitations [1]:

- Since all Kotlin exceptions are unchecked while Swift only has checked errors, a Kotlin method that throws and is called from Swift/Objective-C should be marked with `@Throws`, listing the "expected" exception classes [1].
- When compiling to a Swift/Objective-C framework, non-`suspend` functions that have or inherit `@Throws` are represented as `NSError*`-producing methods in Objective-C and as `throws` methods in Swift. `suspend` function representations always have an `NSError*`/`Error` parameter in the completion handler [1].
- If a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C throws an exception that is an instance of one of the `@Throws`-specified classes (or their subclasses), the exception is propagated as an `NSError`. Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination [1].
- `suspend` functions without `@Throws` propagate only `CancellationException` (as `NSError`). Non-`suspend` functions without `@Throws` don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all [1].

Note: the reverse translation is not implemented — Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing [1].

This should significantly improve multiplatform development for Apple targets. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

The key features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

evidence.query: How are Kotlin exceptions exposed to Swift and Objective-C callers?

chunks.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.

Hide Kotlin declarations from Objective-C and Swift

To make your Kotlin code more Swift/Objective-C-friendly, use the @HiddenFromObjC annotation to hide a Kotlin declaration from Objective-C and Swift. It disables the function or property export to Objective-C.

Alternatively, you can mark Kotlin declarations with the internal modifier to restrict their visibility in the compilation module. Use @HiddenFromObjC if you want to hide the Kotlin declaration from Objective-C and Swift while keeping it visible to other Kotlin modules.

answers.answer:
Kotlin exceptions are **unchecked**, but Swift/Objective-C only understand checked errors (`NSError`/`throws`). So exposure depends on annotations:

- **Non-suspend functions marked or inheriting `@Throws`** are represented as `NSError*`-producing methods in Objective-C and `throws` methods in Swift [1]. If such a function throws an exception that is an instance of a class listed in `@Throws` (or a subclass), it is propagated as an `NSError` [1].
- **Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination** [1].
- **Non-suspend functions without `@Throws` don’t propagate Kotlin exceptions at all** [1].
- **`suspend` functions** always have an `NSError*`/`Error` parameter in the completion handler; without `@Throws`, they propagate only `CancellationException` (as `NSError`) [1].

Example:

```kotlin
@Throws(IOException::class)
fun readFile() { throw IOException() }
```

When called from Swift/Obj-C, `IOException` can surface as an `NSError`/thrown error. Without `@Throws`, it would not propagate for a non-suspend function.

Note: the reverse direction is not implemented — Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods are not imported into Kotlin as exception-throwing [1].

candidates.text:
Extensions and category members

Members of Objective-C categories and Swift extensions are generally imported to Kotlin as extensions. That's why these declarations can't be overridden in Kotlin, and the extension initializers aren't available as Kotlin constructors.

Currently, there are two exceptions. This means that you can override methods that subclass from NSView or UIView.

Kotlin extensions to "regular" Kotlin classes are imported to Swift and Objective-C as extensions and category members, respectively. Kotlin extensions to other types are treated as top-level declarations with an additional receiver parameter. These types include:

The Objective-C libraries import is in Beta . All Kotlin declarations generated by the cinterop tool from Objective-C libraries should have the @ExperimentalForeignApi annotation.

candidates.text:
Initializers

A Swift/Objective-C initializer is imported to Kotlin as constructors or as factory methods named create . The latter happens with initializers declared in the Objective-C category or as a Swift extension, because Kotlin has no concept of extension constructors.

Before importing Swift initializers to Kotlin, don't forget to annotate them with @objc .

Kotlin constructors are imported as initializers to Swift/Objective-C.

candidates.text:
Method names translation

Generally, Swift argument labels and Objective-C selector pieces are mapped to Kotlin parameter names. These two concepts have different semantics, so sometimes Swift/Objective-C methods can be imported with a clashing Kotlin signature. In this case, the clashing methods can be called from Kotlin using named arguments, for example:

[player moveTo:LEFT byMeters:17]
[player moveTo:UP byInches:42]

In Kotlin, it's:

player.moveTo(LEFT, byMeters = 17)
player.moveTo(UP, byInches = 42)

Here's how the kotlin.Any functions are mapped to Swift/Objective-C:

Kotlin | Swift | Objective-C
equals() | isEquals(_:) | isEquals:
hashCode() | hash | hash
toString() | description | description

See an example with data classes in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.

answers.answer:
Kotlin's exception model doesn't map directly onto Swift/Objective-C's, so the exposure depends on annotations and function type.

**Key rules**

- All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked (caught at runtime), while Swift has compile-time checked errors [1].
- When Swift/Objective-C calls a Kotlin function that throws, the Kotlin function **should be marked with `@Throws`**, listing the "expected" exception classes [1].
- When compiled to a Swift/Objective-C framework, **non-`suspend` functions that have or inherit `@Throws`** are exposed as `NSError*`-producing methods in Objective-C and `throws` methods in Swift [1].
- **`suspend` functions** always have an `NSError*` / `Error` parameter in the completion handler [1].
- If a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C throws an exception that is an instance of a `@Throws`-listed class (or subclass), it's propagated as an `NSError`. **Any other Kotlin exception reaching Swift/Objective-C is treated as unhandled and causes program termination** [1].
- **`suspend` functions without `@Throws`** propagate only `CancellationException` (as `NSError`). **Non-`suspend` functions without `@Throws` don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all** [1].
- The reverse direction is **not implemented**: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported into Kotlin as exception-throwing [1].

**Example**

```kotlin
@Throws(IOException::class)
fun writeToFile() {
    throw IOException()
}
```

With `@Throws`, the method appears in Swift as `throws` and in Objective-C as an `NSError**`-producing method; an `IOException` (or subclass) is converted to `NSError`. Without `@Throws` on a non-`suspend` function, the exception isn't propagated to the caller [1].

Note that the docs also point to a Kotlin-Swift interopedia example for further detail [2].

candidates.text:
Hide Kotlin declarations from Objective-C and Swift

To make your Kotlin code more Swift/Objective-C-friendly, use the @HiddenFromObjC annotation to hide a Kotlin declaration from Objective-C and Swift. It disables the function or property export to Objective-C.

Alternatively, you can mark Kotlin declarations with the internal modifier to restrict their visibility in the compilation module. Use @HiddenFromObjC if you want to hide the Kotlin declaration from Objective-C and Swift while keeping it visible to other Kotlin modules.

See an example in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

candidates.text:
Extensions and category members

Members of Objective-C categories and Swift extensions are generally imported to Kotlin as extensions. That's why these declarations can't be overridden in Kotlin, and the extension initializers aren't available as Kotlin constructors.

Currently, there are two exceptions. Starting with Kotlin 1.8.20, category members that are declared in the same headers as the NSView class (from the AppKit framework) or UIView classes (from the UIKit framework) are imported as members of these classes. This means that you can override methods that subclass from NSView or UIView.

Kotlin extensions to "regular" Kotlin classes are imported to Swift and Objective-C as extensions and category members, respectively. Kotlin extensions to other types are treated as top-level declarations with an additional receiver parameter. These types include:

The Objective-C libraries import is in Beta . All Kotlin declarations generated by the cinterop tool from Objective-C libraries should have the @ExperimentalForeignApi annotation.

Native platform libraries shipped with Kotlin/Native (like Foundation, UIKit, and POSIX) require opt-in only for some APIs.

candidates.text:
Initializers

A Swift/Objective-C initializer is imported to Kotlin as constructors or as factory methods named create . The latter happens with initializers declared in the Objective-C category or as a Swift extension, because Kotlin has no concept of extension constructors.

Before importing Swift initializers to Kotlin, don't forget to annotate them with @objc .

Kotlin constructors are imported as initializers to Swift/Objective-C.

candidates.text:
Method names translation

Generally, Swift argument labels and Objective-C selector pieces are mapped to Kotlin parameter names. These two concepts have different semantics, so sometimes Swift/Objective-C methods can be imported with a clashing Kotlin signature. In this case, the clashing methods can be called from Kotlin using named arguments, for example:

[player moveTo:LEFT byMeters:17]
[player moveTo:UP byInches:42]

In Kotlin, it's:

player.moveTo(LEFT, byMeters = 17)
player.moveTo(UP, byInches = 42)

Here's how the kotlin.Any functions are mapped to Swift/Objective-C:

Kotlin | Swift | Objective-C
equals() | isEquals(_:) | isEquals:
hashCode() | hash | hash
toString() | description | description

See an example with data classes in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

candidates.text:
Interoperability with Swift using Swift export

Kotlin's interoperability with Swift through Swift export is currently in Alpha. Swift export allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

Swift export makes multiplatform development for Apple targets more streamlined. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

Current Swift export features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

candidates.text:
Swift export available by default

Kotlin 2.2.20 introduces experimental support for Swift export. It allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

This should significantly improve multiplatform development for Apple targets. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

The key features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

evidence.query: How are Kotlin exceptions exposed to Swift and Objective-C callers?

chunks.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.
chunks.title: Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C
sections: Interoperability with Swift/Objective-C > Mappings > Errors and exceptions

answers.answer:
Kotlin exceptions are exposed to Swift/Objective-C callers through the `@Throws` annotation.

- All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, whereas Swift has only checked errors handled at compile time. So a Kotlin method that may throw and is called from Swift/Objective-C should be marked with `@Throws`, listing the "expected" exception classes [1].
- When compiling to a Swift/Objective-C framework, non-`suspend` functions with or inheriting `@Throws` are represented as `NSError*`-producing methods in Objective-C and `throws` methods in Swift. `suspend` functions always have an `NSError*`/`Error` parameter in the completion handler [1].
- If a called Kotlin function throws an exception that is an instance of one of the `@Throws`-specified classes (or a subclass), it is propagated as an `NSError`. Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are unhandled and cause program termination [1].
- `suspend` functions without `@Throws` propagate only `CancellationException` as `NSError`. Non-`suspend` functions without `@Throws` don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all [1].
- The reverse translation is not implemented: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods are not imported into Kotlin as exception-throwing [1].

Suspending functions

Kotlin's suspending functions ( suspend ) are presented in the generated Objective-C headers as functions with callbacks, or completion handlers in Swift/Objective-C terminology.

Starting from Swift 5.5, Kotlin's suspend functions are also available for calling from Swift as async functions without using the completion handlers. Currently, this functionality is highly experimental and has certain limitations. See this YouTrack issue for details.

Learn more about the async / await mechanism in the Swift documentation .

See an example and recommendations on third-party libraries that implement the same functionality in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-swift-export.html (normalized source lines 15-23; release unknown; availability unknown)
Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

Concurrency support . You can seamlessly call suspending Kotlin code from Swift and export kotlinx.coroutines flows as Swift's AsyncSequence out of the box.

[5] Swift export — Interoperability with Swift using Swift export
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/native-swift-export.html (normalized source lines 1-13; release unknown; availability unknown)
Interoperability with Swift using Swift export

Kotlin's interoperability with Swift through Swift export is currently in Alpha. Swift export allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

Swift export makes multiplatform development for Apple targets more streamlined. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

Current Swift export features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

candidates.text:
New export of suspend function with JsExport

Previously, the @JsExport annotation did not allow exporting suspend functions (or classes and interfaces containing such functions) to JavaScript. You had to manually wrap each suspend function, which was cumbersome and prone to errors.

Starting with Kotlin 2.3.0, suspend functions can be exported directly to JavaScript using the @JsExport annotation.

Enabling suspend function exports reduces boilerplate and improves interoperability between Kotlin/JS and JavaScript/TypeScript (JS/TS). Kotlin's async functions can now be called directly from JS/TS without extra code.

candidates.text:
Coroutine dispatchers

By default, when you call a Kotlin suspending function from Swift or use the asAsyncSequence function, Kotlin creates a coroutine context that uses the Dispatchers.Default dispatcher and executes the exported code there.

To run the exported code on a different dispatcher , use the withContext() function to switch the coroutine context in Kotlin. For example:

suspend fun runOnMain(): Int = withContext(Dispatchers.Main) {
    delay(10L)
    42
}

candidates.text:
Swift export available by default

Kotlin 2.2.20 introduces experimental support for Swift export. It allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

This should significantly improve multiplatform development for Apple targets. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

The key features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

candidates.text:
Current limitations

Swift export currently works only in projects that use direct integration to connect the iOS framework to the Xcode project. This is a standard configuration for Kotlin Multiplatform projects created with the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin in IntelliJ IDEA or through the web wizard .

Other known issues:

Types that inherit from List , Set , or Map are ignored during the export ( KT-80416 ).

Inheritors of List , Set , or Map cannot be instantiated on the Swift side ( KT-80417 ).

When exported to Swift, Kotlin generic type parameters are type-erased to their upper bounds.

No IDE migration tips or automation are available.

Starting from Swift 5.5, Kotlin's suspend functions are also available for calling from Swift as async functions without using the completion handlers. Currently, this functionality is highly experimental and has certain limitations. See this YouTrack issue for details.

Learn more about the async / await mechanism in the Swift documentation .

See an example and recommendations on third-party libraries that implement the same functionality in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

candidates.text:
New export of suspend function with JsExport

Previously, the @JsExport annotation did not allow exporting suspend functions (or classes and interfaces containing such functions) to JavaScript. You had to manually wrap each suspend function, which was cumbersome and prone to errors.

candidates.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.

candidates.text:
Current limitations

Swift export currently works only in projects that use direct integration to connect the iOS framework to the Xcode project. This is a standard configuration for Kotlin Multiplatform projects created with the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin in IntelliJ IDEA or through the web wizard .

Other known issues:

Types that inherit from List , Set , or Map are ignored during the export ( KT-80416 ).

Inheritors of List , Set , or Map cannot be instantiated on the Swift side ( KT-80417 ).

When exported to Swift, Kotlin generic type parameters are type-erased to their upper bounds.

No IDE migration tips or automation are available.

candidates.text:
Swift export available by default

Kotlin 2.2.20 introduces experimental support for Swift export. It allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

This should significantly improve multiplatform development for Apple targets. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

The key features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

candidates.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.

candidates.text:
Current limitations

Swift export currently works only in projects that use direct integration to connect the iOS framework to the Xcode project. This is a standard configuration for Kotlin Multiplatform projects created with the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin in IntelliJ IDEA or through the web wizard .

Other known issues:

Types that inherit from List , Set , or Map are ignored during the export ( KT-80416 ).

Inheritors of List , Set , or Map cannot be instantiated on the Swift side ( KT-80417 ).

When exported to Swift, Kotlin generic type parameters are type-erased to their upper bounds.

No IDE migration tips or automation are available.

chunks.text:
Suspending functions

Kotlin's suspending functions ( suspend ) are presented in the generated Objective-C headers as functions with callbacks, or completion handlers in Swift/Objective-C terminology.

Starting from Swift 5.5, Kotlin's suspend functions are also available for calling from Swift as async functions without using the completion handlers. Currently, this functionality is highly experimental and has certain limitations. See this YouTrack issue for details.

Learn more about the async / await mechanism in the Swift documentation .

See an example and recommendations on third-party libraries that implement the same functionality in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

chunks.text:
Coroutine dispatchers

By default, when you call a Kotlin suspending function from Swift or use the asAsyncSequence function, Kotlin creates a coroutine context that uses the Dispatchers.Default dispatcher and executes the exported code there.

To run the exported code on a different dispatcher , use the withContext() function to switch the coroutine context in Kotlin. For example:

suspend fun runOnMain(): Int = withContext(Dispatchers.Main) {
    delay(10L)
    42
}

candidates.text:
New export of suspend function with JsExport

Previously, the @JsExport annotation did not allow exporting suspend functions (or classes and interfaces containing such functions) to JavaScript. You had to manually wrap each suspend function, which was cumbersome and prone to errors.

Starting with Kotlin 2.3.0, suspend functions can be exported directly to JavaScript using the @JsExport annotation.

Enabling suspend function exports reduces boilerplate and improves interoperability between Kotlin/JS and JavaScript/TypeScript (JS/TS). Kotlin's async functions can now be called directly from JS/TS without extra code.

chunks.text:
Suspending functions

Kotlin's suspending functions ( suspend ) are presented in the generated Objective-C headers as functions with callbacks, or completion handlers in Swift/Objective-C terminology.

Starting from Swift 5.5, Kotlin's suspend functions are also available for calling from Swift as async functions without using the completion handlers. Currently, this functionality is highly experimental and has certain limitations. See this YouTrack issue for details.

Learn more about the async / await mechanism in the Swift documentation .

See an example and recommendations on third-party libraries that implement the same functionality in the Kotlin-Swift interopedia .

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

Concurrency support . You can seamlessly call suspending Kotlin code from Swift and export kotlinx.coroutines flows as Swift's AsyncSequence out of the box.

chunks.text:
Coroutine dispatchers

By default, when you call a Kotlin suspending function from Swift or use the asAsyncSequence function, Kotlin creates a coroutine context that uses the Dispatchers.Default dispatcher and executes the exported code there.

To run the exported code on a different dispatcher , use the withContext() function to switch the coroutine context in Kotlin. For example:

suspend fun runOnMain(): Int = withContext(Dispatchers.Main) {
    delay(10L)
    42
}

answers.answer:
Swift export maps Kotlin `suspend` functions (and suspend functional types) to Swift's idiomatic `async` counterparts, so you call them with `await` rather than completion handlers:

```kotlin
// Kotlin
suspend fun hello(): String {
    delay(1000)
    return "Hello Swift!"
}
```

```swift
// Swift
let msg = try await hello()
```

[1][2]

A few caveats:

- This behavior belongs to **Swift export**, which is distinct from the older Objective-C interop path. Under Objective-C interop, suspend functions are exposed via completion handlers, with `async` callable from Swift 5.5 onward but described as highly experimental and limited [3].
- By default the exported code runs in a coroutine context using `Dispatchers.Default`; use `withContext()` in Kotlin to change the dispatcher [5].
- Feature availability and stability vary by version and feature status; the snippets do not guarantee compatibility with other releases [1][2][4].

candidates.text:
New export of suspend function with JsExport

Previously, the @JsExport annotation did not allow exporting suspend functions (or classes and interfaces containing such functions) to JavaScript. You had to manually wrap each suspend function, which was cumbersome and prone to errors.

How to enable Swift export

The feature is currently Experimental and works only in projects that use direct integration to connect the iOS framework to the Xcode project. This is a standard configuration for multiplatform projects created with the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin in IntelliJ IDEA or through the web wizard .

To try out Swift export, configure your Xcode project:

In Xcode, open the project settings.

On the Build Phases tab, locate the Run Script phase with the embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode task.

Adjust the script to feature the embedSwiftExportForXcode task instead in the run script phase:

./gradlew :<Shared module name>:embedSwiftExportForXcode

Build the project. Swift modules are generated in the build output directory.

candidates.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.

candidates.text:
Swift export available by default

Kotlin 2.2.20 introduces experimental support for Swift export. It allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

This should significantly improve multiplatform development for Apple targets. For example, if you have a Kotlin module with top-level functions, Swift export enables clean, module-specific imports, removing the confusing Objective-C underscores and mangled names.

The key features are:

Multi-module support . Each Kotlin module is exported as a separate Swift module, simplifying function calls.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Type aliases . Kotlin type aliases are exported and preserved in Swift, improving readability.

Enhanced nullability for primitives . Unlike Objective-C interop, which required boxing types like Int? into wrapper classes like KotlinInt to preserve nullability, Swift export converts nullability information directly.

Overloads . You can call Kotlin's overloaded functions in Swift without ambiguity.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Module name customization . You can customize the resulting Swift module names in the Gradle configuration of your Kotlin project.

candidates.text:
How to enable Swift export

The feature is currently Experimental and works only in projects that use direct integration to connect the iOS framework to the Xcode project. This is a standard configuration for multiplatform projects created with the Kotlin Multiplatform plugin in IntelliJ IDEA or through the web wizard .

To try out Swift export, configure your Xcode project:

In Xcode, open the project settings.

On the Build Phases tab, locate the Run Script phase with the embedAndSignAppleFrameworkForXcode task.

Adjust the script to feature the embedSwiftExportForXcode task instead in the run script phase:

./gradlew :<Shared module name>:embedSwiftExportForXcode

Build the project. Swift modules are generated in the build output directory.

candidates.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.

answers.answer:
Swift export exposes Kotlin `suspend` functions as Swift `async` functions, so you call them from Swift with `await` [1][3]. Suspend functional types are exported as async counterparts as well [1][2].

Kotlin:
```kotlin
suspend fun hello(): String {
    delay(1000)
    return "Hello Swift! This is Kotlin."
}
```

Swift:
```swift
let msg = try await hello()
```
[1][2]

Per the mapping table, `suspend fun` → `async` [3].

Notes/caveats:
- These snippets describe Swift export; the older Swift/Objective-C interop presents suspend functions as completion-handler functions, with Swift `async` support described as experimental and limited [4].
- By default, calling a Kotlin suspend function from Swift runs on `Dispatchers.Default`; use `withContext(...)` in Kotlin to switch dispatchers [5].
- Availability may depend on feature status and version; the references do not establish compatibility beyond what they state [1][2].

candidates.text:

Kotlin 2.2.20 introduces experimental support for Swift export. It allows you to export Kotlin sources directly and call Kotlin code from Swift idiomatically, eliminating the need for Objective-C headers.

Package support . Kotlin packages are explicitly preserved during export, avoiding naming conflicts in the generated Swift code.

Flattened package structure . You can translate Kotlin packages into Swift enums, removing the package prefix from generated Swift code.

Kotlin's suspending functions ( suspend ) are presented in the generated Objective-C headers as functions with callbacks, or completion handlers in Swift/Objective-C terminology.

Starting from Swift 5.5, Kotlin's suspend functions are also available for calling from Swift as async functions without using the completion handlers. Currently, this functionality is highly experimental and has certain limitations. See this YouTrack issue for details.

chunks.text:
Coroutine dispatchers

By default, when you call a Kotlin suspending function from Swift or use the asAsyncSequence function, Kotlin creates a coroutine context that uses the Dispatchers.Default dispatcher and executes the exported code there.

    delay(10L)
    42
}

candidates.text:
Errors and exceptions

All Kotlin exceptions are unchecked, meaning that errors are caught at runtime. However, Swift has only checked errors that are handled at compile time. So, if Swift or Objective-C code calls a Kotlin method that throws an exception, the Kotlin method should be marked with the @Throws annotation, specifying a list of "expected" exception classes.

When compiling to the Swift/Objective-C framework, non- suspend functions that have or inherit the @Throws annotation are represented as NSError* -producing methods in Objective-C and as throws methods in Swift. Representations for suspend functions always have an NSError* / Error parameter in the completion handler.

When a Kotlin function called from Swift/Objective-C code throws an exception which is an instance of one of the classes specified with @Throws or their subclasses, the exception is propagated as an NSError . Other Kotlin exceptions reaching Swift/Objective-C are considered unhandled and cause program termination.

suspend functions without @Throws propagate only CancellationException (as NSError ). Non- suspend functions without @Throws don't propagate Kotlin exceptions at all.

Note that the opposite reversed translation is not implemented yet: Swift/Objective-C error-throwing methods aren't imported to Kotlin as exception-throwing.

External declarations

External JavaScript code is not visible in Kotlin by default. To use JavaScript code in Kotlin, you can describe its API with external declarations.

candidates.text:
external modifier

To tell Kotlin that a certain declaration is written in pure JavaScript, you should mark it with the external modifier. When the compiler sees such a declaration, it assumes that the implementation for the corresponding class, function or property is provided externally (by the developer or via an npm dependency ), and therefore does not try to generate any JavaScript code from the declaration. This is also why external declarations can't have a body. For example:

external fun alert(message: Any?): Unit

external class Node {
    val firstChild: Node

    fun append(child: Node): Node

    fun removeChild(child: Node): Node

    // etc
}

external val window: Window

Note that the external modifier is inherited by nested declarations. This is why in the example Node class, there is no external modifier before member functions and properties.

The external modifier is only allowed on package-level declarations. You can't declare an external member of a non- external class.

}

If you have explicitly set your module kind to be plain , Kotlin creates an object that contains all Kotlin declarations from the current module. This is done to prevent spoiling the global object. Calling the function directly like this is not applicable when you compile your Kotlin module to JavaScript modules like UMD (the default setting for both browser and nodejs targets), ESM , CommonJS , or AMD . answers.answer:
In Kotlin/Wasm, you describe an existing JavaScript API using **`external` declarations** — they declare the shape/signature without providing a body, so Kotlin can call the JavaScript code [1][2].

Common forms:

**External function**
```kotlin
external fun greet(name: String)
```
JavaScript:
```js
function greet (name) {
    console.log("Hello, " + name + "!");
}
```
External functions have no bodies and are called like regular Kotlin functions [2].

**External class**
```kotlin
external class Rectangle(height: Double, width: Double) : JsAny {
    val height: Double
    val width: Double
    fun area(): Double
}
```
All declarations inside an external class are implicitly external [4].

**External interface** (for describing the shape of a JavaScript object)
```kotlin
external interface User : JsAny {
    val name: String
    val age: Int
}

external fun createUser(name: String, age: Int): User
```
External interfaces have no runtime type information and are compile-time-only [5].

**Importing from a JavaScript module**

By default, external declarations correspond to the JavaScript global scope. To import from a specific module, annotate the file with `@JsModule`:
```kotlin
@file:JsModule("./users.mjs")

external val maxUsers: Int

external class User : JsAny {
    constructor(username: String)
    val username: String
}
```
All external declarations in the file are then imported from that module [3].

**Version caveats:** The cited docs are Kotlin/Wasm JS interop snapshots with unknown release/availability; feature availability may differ across versions and platforms (e.g., Kotlin/JS has its own `external` semantics) [1][2][3][4][5].

If you have explicitly set your module kind to be plain , Kotlin creates an object that contains all Kotlin declarations from the current module. This is done to prevent spoiling the global object. This means that for a module myModule , all declarations are available to JavaScript via the myModule object. For example:

fun foo() = "Hello"

This function can be called from JavaScript like this:

alert(myModule.foo());

Calling the function directly like this is not applicable when you compile your Kotlin module to JavaScript modules like UMD (the default setting for both browser and nodejs targets), ESM , CommonJS , or AMD . In these cases, your declarations are exposed according to the chosen JavaScript module system. For example, when using UMD, ESM, or CommonJS, your call site would look like this:

alert(require('myModule').foo());

candidates.text:
Use JavaScript code from Kotlin

Kotlin was first designed for easy interoperation with the Java platform: it sees Java classes as Kotlin classes, and Java sees Kotlin classes as Java classes.

However, JavaScript is a dynamically typed language, which means it does not check types at compile time. You can freely talk to JavaScript from Kotlin via dynamic types. If you want to use the full power of the Kotlin type system, you can create external declarations for JavaScript libraries which will be understood by the Kotlin compiler and the surrounding tooling.

candidates.text:
Package structure

For most of the module systems (CommonJS, Plain, and UMD), Kotlin exposes its package structure to JavaScript. Unless you define your declarations in the root package, you have to use fully qualified names in JavaScript. For example:

package my.qualified.packagename

fun foo() = "Hello"

For example, when using UMD or CommonJS, your call site could look like this:

alert(require('myModule').my.qualified.packagename.foo())

When using plain as a module system setting, the call site would be:

alert(myModule.my.qualified.packagename.foo());

When targeting ECMAScript Modules (ESM), package information is not preserved to improve the application bundle size and match the typical layout of ESM packages. In this case, the consumption of the Kotlin declarations with ES modules looks like this:

import { foo } from 'myModule';

alert(foo());

answers.answer:
Use `external` declarations: they describe an existing JavaScript API's shape to Kotlin and have no Kotlin bodies [1][2].

```kotlin
external fun greet(name: String)          // existing JS function

external class Rectangle(height: Double, width: Double) : JsAny {
    val height: Double
    val width: Double
    fun area(): Double                    // members are implicitly external
}

external interface User : JsAny {         // describes a JS object shape
    val name: String
    val age: Int
}
```

So instead of implementing the API, you only declare it, then call it like ordinary Kotlin code [2]. By default, external declarations refer to the JavaScript global scope; annotate the file with `@JsModule("...")` to import declarations from a specific module instead [3].

Note: this guidance is from the Kotlin/Wasm JS interop docs; release and availability are unknown in the provided snapshot, so version compatibility isn't guaranteed [1][2][3].

candidates.text:
external modifier

To tell Kotlin that a certain declaration is written in pure JavaScript, you should mark it with the external modifier. When the compiler sees such a declaration, it assumes that the implementation for the corresponding class, function or property is provided externally (by the developer or via an npm dependency ), and therefore does not try to generate any JavaScript code from the declaration. This is also why external declarations can't have a body. For example:

external fun alert(message: Any?): Unit

external class Node {
    val firstChild: Node

    fun append(child: Node): Node

    fun removeChild(child: Node): Node

    // etc
}

external val window: Window

Note that the external modifier is inherited by nested declarations. This is why in the example Node class, there is no external modifier before member functions and properties.

The external modifier is only allowed on package-level declarations. You can't declare an external member of a non- external class.

candidates.text:
Declare parameters with default values

If you are writing an external declaration for a JavaScript function which has a parameter with a default value, use definedExternally . This delegates the generation of the default values to the JavaScript function itself:

external fun myFunWithOptionalArgs(
    x: Int,
    y: String = definedExternally,
    z: String = definedExternally
)

With this external declaration, you can call myFunWithOptionalArgs with one required argument and two optional arguments, where the default values are calculated by the JavaScript implementation of myFunWithOptionalArgs .

candidates.text:
Using JNI with Kotlin

To declare a function that is implemented in native (C or C++) code, you need to mark it with the external modifier:

external fun foo(x: Int): Double

The rest of the procedure works in exactly the same way as in Java.

You can also mark property getters and setters as external :

var myProperty: String
    external get
    external set

Behind the scenes, this will create two functions getMyProperty and setMyProperty , both marked as external .

answers.answer:
Use `external` declarations to describe the existing JavaScript API's shape to Kotlin; the implementation stays in JavaScript [1].

Examples:

- External function:
```kotlin
external fun createUser(name: String, age: Int): User
```
[2]

- External interface (compile-time-only shape description, no runtime type info):
```kotlin
external interface User : JsAny {
    val name: String
    val age: Int
}
```
[2]

- External class:
```kotlin
external class Rectangle(height: Double, width: Double) : JsAny {
    val height: Double
    val width: Double
    fun area(): Double
}
```
All declarations inside an external class are implicitly external [3].

Caveat: The `JsAny` supertype and interface restrictions shown are from the Kotlin/Wasm JS interop docs [2][3]. The general Kotlin/JS external-interface docs describe external interfaces without requiring `JsAny` [4], so exact syntax may depend on the target (Wasm vs. JS) and version.

JsReference type

Kotlin values can be passed to JavaScript as opaque references using the JsReference type.

For example, if you want to expose this Kotlin class User to JavaScript:

class User(var name: String)

You can use the toJsReference() function to create JsReference<User> and return it to JavaScript:

@JsExport
fun createUser(name: String): JsReference<User> {
    return User(name).toJsReference()
}

These references aren't directly available in JavaScript and behave like empty frozen JavaScript objects. To operate on these objects, you need to export more functions to JavaScript using the get() method where you unwrap the reference value:

@JsExport
fun setUserName(user: JsReference<User>, name: String) {
    user.get().name = name
}

[2] Kotlin/Wasm JavaScript interoperability — Interoperability with JavaScript > Kotlin/Wasm and Kotlin/JS interoperability differences
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/wasm-js-interop.html (normalized source lines 393-410; release unknown; availability unknown)
Kotlin/Wasm and Kotlin/JS interoperability differences

Although Kotlin/Wasm interoperability shares similarities with Kotlin/JS interoperability, there are key differences to consider:

 | Kotlin/Wasm | Kotlin/JS
External enums | Doesn't support external enum classes. | Supports external enum classes.
Type extensions | Doesn't support non-external types to extend external types. | Supports non-external types.
JsName annotation | Only has an effect when annotating external declarations. | Can be used to change names of regular non-external declarations.
js() function | js("code") function calls are allowed as a single expression body of package-level functions. | The js("code") function can be called in any context and returns a dynamic value.
Module systems | Supports ES modules only. There is no analog of the @JsNonModule annotation. Provides its exports as properties on the default object. Allows exporting package-level functions only. | Supports ES modules and legacy module systems. Provides named ESM exports. Allows exporting classes and objects.
Types | Applies stricter type restrictions uniformly to all interop declarations external , = js("code") , and @JsExport . Allows a select number of built-in Kotlin types and JsAny subtypes . | Allows all types in external declarations. Restricts types that can be used in @JsExport .
Long | Type corresponds to JavaScript BigInt . | Visible as a custom class in JavaScript.
Arrays | Not supported in interop directly yet. You can use the new JsArray type instead. | Implemented as JavaScript arrays.
Other types | Requires JsReference<> to pass Kotlin objects to JavaScript. | Allows the use of non-external Kotlin class types in external declarations.
Exception handling | You can catch any JavaScript exception with the JsException and Throwable types. | Can catch JavaScript Error using the Throwable type. It can catch any JavaScript exception using the dynamic type.
Dynamic types | Does not support the dynamic type. Use JsAny instead (see sample code below). | Supports the dynamic type.

Kotlin/JS dynamic type for interoperability with untyped or loosely typed objects is not supported in Kotlin/Wasm. Instead of the dynamic type, you can use the JsAny type:

[3] Kotlin/Wasm JavaScript interoperability — Interoperability with JavaScript > Type correspondence
https://kotlinlang.org/docs/wasm-js-interop.html (normalized source lines 280-298; release unknown; availability unknown)
Type correspondence

Kotlin/Wasm allows only certain types in signatures of JavaScript interop declarations. These limitations apply uniformly to declarations with external , = js("code") or @JsExport .

See how Kotlin types correspond to JavaScript types:

Kotlin | JavaScript
Byte , Short , Int , Char , UByte , UShort , UInt , | Number
Float , Double , | Number
Long , ULong , | BigInt
Boolean , | Boolean
String , | String
Unit in return position | undefined
Function type, for example (String) -> Int | Function
JsAny and subtypes | Any JavaScript value
JsReference | Opaque reference to Kotlin object
Other types | Not supported

You can use nullable versions of these types as well.

chunks.text:
Kotlin/Wasm and Kotlin/JS interoperability differences

Although Kotlin/Wasm interoperability shares similarities with Kotlin/JS interoperability, there are key differences to consider:

 | Kotlin/Wasm | Kotlin/JS
External enums | Doesn't support external enum classes. | Supports external enum classes.
Type extensions | Doesn't support non-external types to extend external types. | Supports non-external types.
JsName annotation | Only has an effect when annotating external declarations. | Can be used to change names of regular non-external declarations.
js() function | js("code") function calls are allowed as a single expression body of package-level functions. | The js("code") function can be called in any context and returns a dynamic value.
Module systems | Supports ES modules only. There is no analog of the @JsNonModule annotation. Provides its exports as properties on the default object. Allows exporting package-level functions only. | Supports ES modules and legacy module systems. Provides named ESM exports. Allows exporting classes and objects.
Types | Applies stricter type restrictions uniformly to all interop declarations external , = js("code") , and @JsExport . Allows a select number of built-in Kotlin types and JsAny subtypes . | Allows all types in external declarations. Restricts types that can be used in @JsExport .
Long | Type corresponds to JavaScript BigInt . | Visible as a custom class in JavaScript.
Arrays | Not supported in interop directly yet. You can use the new JsArray type instead. | Implemented as JavaScript arrays.
Other types | Requires JsReference<> to pass Kotlin objects to JavaScript. | Allows the use of non-external Kotlin class types in external declarations.
Exception handling | You can catch any JavaScript exception with the JsException and Throwable types. | Can catch JavaScript Error using the Throwable type. It can catch any JavaScript exception using the dynamic type.
Dynamic types | Does not support the dynamic type. Use JsAny instead (see sample code below). | Supports the dynamic type.

Kotlin/JS dynamic type for interoperability with untyped or loosely typed objects is not supported in Kotlin/Wasm. Instead of the dynamic type, you can use the JsAny type:

Type correspondence

Kotlin/Wasm allows only certain types in signatures of JavaScript interop declarations. These limitations apply uniformly to declarations with external , = js("code") or @JsExport .

See how Kotlin types correspond to JavaScript types:

Kotlin | JavaScript
Byte , Short , Int , Char , UByte , UShort , UInt , | Number
Float , Double , | Number
Long , ULong , | BigInt
Boolean , | Boolean
String , | String
Unit in return position | undefined
Function type, for example (String) -> Int | Function
JsAny and subtypes | Any JavaScript value
JsReference | Opaque reference to Kotlin object
Other types | Not supported

You can use nullable versions of these types as well.

JsReference type

Kotlin values can be passed to JavaScript as opaque references using the JsReference type.

For example, if you want to expose this Kotlin class User to JavaScript:

class User(var name: String)

You can use the toJsReference() function to create JsReference<User> and return it to JavaScript:

@JsExport
fun createUser(name: String): JsReference<User> {
    return User(name).toJsReference()
}

These references aren't directly available in JavaScript and behave like empty frozen JavaScript objects. To operate on these objects, you need to export more functions to JavaScript using the get() method where you unwrap the reference value:

@JsExport
fun setUserName(user: JsReference<User>, name: String) {
    user.get().name = name
}

For example, if you want to expose this Kotlin class User to JavaScript:

chunks.text:
Kotlin/Wasm and Kotlin/JS interoperability differences

Although Kotlin/Wasm interoperability shares similarities with Kotlin/JS interoperability, there are key differences to consider:

 | Kotlin/Wasm | Kotlin/JS
External enums | Doesn't support external enum classes. | Supports external enum classes.
Type extensions | Doesn't support non-external types to extend external types. | Supports non-external types.
JsName annotation | Only has an effect when annotating external declarations. | Can be used to change names of regular non-external declarations.
js() function | js("code") function calls are allowed as a single expression body of package-level functions. | The js("code") function can be called in any context and returns a dynamic value.
Module systems | Supports ES modules only. There is no analog of the @JsNonModule annotation. Provides its exports as properties on the default object. Allows exporting package-level functions only. | Supports ES modules and legacy module systems. Provides named ESM exports. Allows exporting classes and objects.
Types | Applies stricter type restrictions uniformly to all interop declarations external , = js("code") , and @JsExport . Allows a select number of built-in Kotlin types and JsAny subtypes . | Allows all types in external declarations. Restricts types that can be used in @JsExport .
Long | Type corresponds to JavaScript BigInt . | Visible as a custom class in JavaScript.
Arrays | Not supported in interop directly yet. You can use the new JsArray type instead. | Implemented as JavaScript arrays.
Other types | Requires JsReference<> to pass Kotlin objects to JavaScript. | Allows the use of non-external Kotlin class types in external declarations.
Exception handling | You can catch any JavaScript exception with the JsException and Throwable types. | Can catch JavaScript Error using the Throwable type. It can catch any JavaScript exception using the dynamic type.
Dynamic types | Does not support the dynamic type. Use JsAny instead (see sample code below). | Supports the dynamic type.

Kotlin/JS dynamic type for interoperability with untyped or loosely typed objects is not supported in Kotlin/Wasm. Instead of the dynamic type, you can use the JsAny type:

chunks.text:
Type correspondence

Kotlin/Wasm allows only certain types in signatures of JavaScript interop declarations. These limitations apply uniformly to declarations with external , = js("code") or @JsExport .

See how Kotlin types correspond to JavaScript types:

Kotlin | JavaScript
Byte , Short , Int , Char , UByte , UShort , UInt , | Number
Float , Double , | Number
Long , ULong , | BigInt
Boolean , | Boolean
String , | String
Unit in return position | undefined
Function type, for example (String) -> Int | Function
JsAny and subtypes | Any JavaScript value
JsReference | Opaque reference to Kotlin object
Other types | Not supported

You can use nullable versions of these types as well.

candidates.text:
Kotlin/Wasm treats calls to the js() function in a special way, and the implementation has some restrictions:

A js() function call must be provided with a string literal argument.

A js() function call must be the only expression in the function body.

The js() function is only allowed to be called from package-level functions.

The function return type must be provided explicitly.

Types are restricted, similar to external fun .

The Kotlin compiler puts the code string into a function in the generated JavaScript file and imports it into WebAssembly format. The Kotlin compiler doesn't verify these JavaScript snippets. If there are JavaScript syntax errors, they are reported when you run your JavaScript code.

JavaScript properties

Consider this global JavaScript variable:

let globalCounter = 0;

You can declare it in Kotlin using external var or val properties:

external var globalCounter: Int

These properties are initialized externally. The properties can't have = value initializers in Kotlin code.

JsReference type

Kotlin values can be passed to JavaScript as opaque references using the JsReference type.

For example, if you want to expose this Kotlin class User to JavaScript:

class User(var name: String)

You can use the toJsReference() function to create JsReference<User> and return it to JavaScript:

@JsExport
fun createUser(name: String): JsReference<User> {
    return User(name).toJsReference()
}

These references aren't directly available in JavaScript and behave like empty frozen JavaScript objects. To operate on these objects, you need to export more functions to JavaScript using the get() method where you unwrap the reference value:

@JsExport
fun setUserName(user: JsReference<User>, name: String) {
    user.get().name = name
}

JsReference type

Kotlin values can be passed to JavaScript as opaque references using the JsReference type.

For example, if you want to expose this Kotlin class User to JavaScript:

class User(var name: String)

You can use the toJsReference() function to create JsReference<User> and return it to JavaScript:

@JsExport
fun createUser(name: String): JsReference<User> {
    return User(name).toJsReference()
}

These references aren't directly available in JavaScript and behave like empty frozen JavaScript objects. To operate on these objects, you need to export more functions to JavaScript using the get() method where you unwrap the reference value:

@JsExport
fun setUserName(user: JsReference<User>, name: String) {
    user.get().name = name
}
